en: Now begins the sixth chapter:
Having thus remained in the householder stage according to rule, the twice-born graduate, with his senses subdued, should dwell in the forest, self-restrained and in accordance with the law. (6.1)

The stage of life characterized by the house is the "householder's stage" (*gṛhāśrama*). "House" (*gṛha*) here means the wife. Having remained there and performed that [stage], the injunction is that one should dwell in the forest. By the use of the suffix *-ktvā* in the word *sthitvā* ("having remained"), the priority of the householder's life over forest-dwelling is shown. The stages of life must be undertaken in their proper sequence; one who has fulfilled the householder's duties is qualified for forest-dwelling. This is stated by adopting the position of cumulative performance (*samuccaya*). Otherwise, it will also be explained that forest-dwelling is possible even for one whose student-life (*brahmacarya*) was unimpaired. "One who has conquered the senses" (*vijitendriya*) means one whose impurities have been ripened away and whose passion has diminished. The words *evaṃ* ("thus") and *vidhivat* ("according to rule") are for the purpose of completing the meter; they have been explained previously in their respective places. This much is enjoined: having completed the householder's life, one should resort to forest-dwelling. 6.1.
But when a householder perceives his own wrinkles and grey hair, and sees the offspring of his offspring, then he should take refuge in the forest. (6.2)

He demonstrates that very point which was stated: "one who has abandoned craving for the enjoyment of sense-objects is qualified [for this practice]. *Valī* is the wrinkling of the skin; *palita* is the graying of the hair. Regarding the term *apatyasyāpatyam*, they say it means "the offspring of one's offspring," that is, the son's son. Even when a daughter has an offspring—a grandson—the learned do not accept this rule [of qualification] even if a son has a daughter born to him.

Others, however, say that the greying of the head and the birth of a grandson are intended as indicators of a particular stage of life. Even one for whom greying does not somehow occur should resort to the forest in old age. Just as one who has fathered a son and possesses black hair is qualified for the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), so too is one who has fathered a grandson and has grey hair. In that case as well, the birth of a son and the state of having black hair serve merely to indicate a specific stage of life.
If these were intended as indicators of a meaning such as "not too quickly" or "not too long," then an authoritative source (*pramāṇa*) for that must be stated. (6.2)
Having abandoned village food and all personal belongings,
and having entrusted his wife to his sons, he should go to the forest, either alone or together with her.

The phrase "having completely renounced" refers to the injunction that from that point forward one should not eat food consisting of rice or barley. This is what is meant by the statement beginning with "eating roots" and so forth. *Paricchada* refers to possessions such as cattle, horses, clothing, vehicles, beds, and the like. If the wife desires it, she may accompany him; otherwise, he goes alone.
Others, however, describe the practice as leaving behind a young wife and departing with an elderly one.

This rule applies when a wife is present: the entrustment of one's duties to one's sons or departing for the forest. Even in her absence, or upon her death, residence in the forest is prescribed by Āpastamba and others in the context of the "re-establishment of the sacred fires" (*punar-ādhāna*). He whose senses are not restless is a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*); another, however, may take a wife again—such is the settled rule. (6.3)
Having taken up the Agnihotra sacrifice and the household implements for the sacred fires, he should depart from the village to the forest and dwell there with his senses restrained. (6.4)

The fires themselves are denoted by the term *agnihotra*. Having taken up—that is, having grasped—the Śrauta fires as well as the domestic (*gṛhya*) equipment for the *agnihotra*, such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles; since there is a rule for the abandonment of domestic equipment, this [passage] is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) specifically for that which is connected to the fires. 6.4.
With various kinds of pure food fit for sages, or with vegetables, roots, and fruits,
he should perform these very great sacrifices according to the prescribed rule.

He should offer these very sacrifices that are prescribed for the householder; he should perform them according to rule. The phrase "according to rule" is a restatement (anuvāda) intended to complete the verse. 6.5.
He should wear either a skin or a garment of bark; he should bathe in the evening as well as in the morning;
and he should always bear matted hair, along with his beard, body hair, and nails. (6.6)

*Carman* refers to the hide of a cow, a deer, or similar animals. *Cīra* is a piece of cloth. *Sāyam* is the time at the close of day; *prage* is at the first dawn of the day. Thus, because of the injunction for bathing in the evening, they say that his meal must be taken at night, since bathing after eating is prohibited. Others, however, say this is incorrect, because the vow of a *snātaka* states: "Therefore, one should bathe after having eaten. Furthermore, in the *Mahābhārata*, this is recorded as a duty for all men. Consequently, bathing three times a day may also be an optional alternative for him. He should not cut his matted hair, beard, body hair, or nails. (6.6)
Whatever his food may be, from that he should offer the bali-oblation and give alms according to his ability;
he should honor one who has come to his hermitage with water, roots, fruits, and alms-food.

It has been stated [in MDh 6.5]: "with the food of sages (*munyanna*). These consist of wild grains such as *nīvāra* and the like, as well as wild vegetables and the like. The word *anna* is generally used for preparations of grain, such as boiled rice, flour-meal, and parched flour; therefore, although vegetables and the like are indeed "food of sages," they are mentioned separately. "Sages" (*muni*) refers to ascetics (*tāpasa*); their food is "the food of sages. One should offer the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*), which involve the duty of cooking in fire. Anticipating the doubt that one should not offer them when subsisting on fruits ripened by time, he says: "whatever his food may be. Whatever he eats—be it flour or other substances—he should offer it according to his ability. As for the *bali* offering, which is prescribed for Indra and Indra’s attendants (*indrāyendrapuruṣebhyaḥ*) and so forth, but excludes the *agnihotra*, in this alternative there is no oblation (*homa*) in the fire.

That is incorrect; since the word *bali* denotes sacrifice (*ijyā*) in general, this applies equally whether [the offering] is made in fire or not in fire. Even if this position were held—that whatever one might eat, that very thing [should be offered] only in fire, and thus an oblation (*homa*) must be performed in fire with cooked food—nevertheless, he will state that vegetables and the like serve that specific purpose alone, while he himself will eat what has ripened naturally in its own time. In any case, even for one who eats only what is ripened by time, the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice remains to be performed in fire alone.

This is a *dvandva* compound beginning with "water" (*ap-*) and so forth. One should honor a traveler who has arrived at the hermitage with water, roots, fruits, and alms such as wild rice (*nīvāra*). || 6.7 ||
He should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas, self-controlled, friendly, and composed;
he should be a giver, never a taker, and compassionate toward all living beings. 6.8

Fearing that one might suspect the cessation of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) and other duties on the grounds that this is a different stage of life (*āśrama*), he says—so that they do not cease—"constantly disciplined" (*nityayukta*). This is not as it is in the householder’s stage; for there, activities for the sake of household affairs also exist, and while those are being performed, there is no Vedic study. "Self-controlled" (*dāntaḥ*) means endowed with restraint, free from intoxication. "Friendly" (*maitraḥ*) means primarily engaged in the conduct of a friend, speaking what is pleasant and beneficial. He is "composed" (*samāhitaḥ*) insofar as he is intent on conforming to the mind of one present before him; even when dependent on others, he would not speak much that is irrelevant or out of context. He is a "giver" (*dātā*) of water and of roots and alms-food. He is "not a receiver" (*anādātā*); for the sake of medicine or other necessities, he should not beg from one who has come from another stage of life. He is "compassionate toward all beings. Compassion is pity. Even though he is compassionate, he should not beg from another for the sake of someone else. (6.8)
And he should offer the Vaitānika Agnihotra according to the rule,
not omitting the Darśa and Paurṇamāsa sacrifices at their proper times through yoga.

A *vitāna* is a sacrificial hall; that which occurs therein is *vaitānika*. One should offer—that is, perform—the *śrauta* rite pertaining to the three sacred fires (*tretāgni*). The word *agnihotra* refers to the substance used for the oblation, such as barley-gruel (*yavāgū*) and so forth, and is not the name of the ritual itself. Consequently, the meaning "one should offer it [the substance] into the Āhavanīya fire" is established by the statement "one offers with the *agnihotra* and so forth. Thus, in the first view, the word *agnihotra* has the same referent as the verb *juhoti* (to offer).

But surely, another alternative has been stated: "having entrusted his wife to his sons" (MDh 6.3). In that case, how can there be eligibility for the *śrauta* rites without her? If you argue that it is "as in the case of one who is away on a journey," [meaning] just as a sacrificer who is away on a journey remains eligible through arrangements even while staying at a distance—such that he remains the performer—so too the wife will give her consent when he is setting out for the forest, and thus their joint eligibility will not be contradicted. That too is untenable. Such a performance would be appropriate if separation from home occurred due to some divine or human calamity, but not by one's own free will. Furthermore, many subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) would be omitted despite the presence of the capacity to perform them. For instance, regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices, it is prescribed that "one should make the wife recite: 'The Veda art thou, acquisition art thou... (TS 1.6.4.4); that would be lost.

Now, it might be argued: "This injunction will apply to the view that they set out together. This too is not tenable, because no specific distinction is mentioned. Furthermore, in the view that the fires are deposited [with the wife], no other method for their disposal is prescribed. Moreover, even in the case of setting out together, this [injunction] is contradicted:
"With pure forest foods fit for sages, gathered by himself, he should separately offer sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) and cooked rice offerings (caru) according to the rule" (MDh 6.11).

The "forest foods" (*āraṇyāni munyannāni*) intended here are wild grains such as *nīvāra* and the like, because the abandonment of domestic utensils is prescribed. Furthermore, sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) made from rice and other grains are ordained in the Veda, and these are domestic products. Nor could the performance of a ritual be completed by substituting any pure forest food for rice, according to the principle of "produced [substitution]" (*utpannanyāya*) or the principle of the injunction regarding rice (*vrīhiśāstravidhinyāya*). Moreover, those [grains] are difficult to procure through a wife. How, then, while the scriptural injunction for lifelong [maintenance of the fires] exists, could there be the abandonment of the sacred fires or of the wife? Therefore, the prescription of another stage of life (*āśrama*) would be inconsistent with the performance of the Vedic sacrificial rites (*vaitānika-karma*).
Effort must be exerted in this matter.

Some say: the term *vaitānika* is applied by way of praise to the very rites prescribed in the *smṛtis*. Furthermore, regarding the *smārta* rites, there is no restrictive rule concerning rice and other grains. For it is traditionally taught therein:
"O King, whatever food a man eats, his deities eat that same food" (Rām 2.95.31).

And therefore, the performance [of rites] with the food of sages (munyanna) would be non-contradictory, and the contradiction with the scriptural injunctions regarding rice (*vrīhi*) and so forth would be resolved. In that case as well, there exists a common qualification (*adhikāra*). What is the resolution for that? Since both are based on Smṛti, it will be sublated in this state.
As for the Vedic statement, "One should sacrifice together with one's wife," that applies only to Vedic rites.

(2) Alternatively, this rule does not pertain to the fire of a householder at all. Rather, Gautama has stated: "Having established the fire according to the Śrāvaṇika rite" (GDh 3.27). Furthermore, the author will state here: "Abiding by the doctrine of the Vaikhānasa" (MDh 6.21). Therefore, these are indeed other rites prescribed by the scriptures. The terms *darśapūrṇamāsa* and so forth are applied there figuratively. Consequently, that establishment of the fire (*ādhāna*) is for one who is without a wife. The disposal of the fires previously acquired through the householder stage is stated [in the verse]: "The sacrificial fires within himself" (MDh 6.25). As for the question, "Since there is a scriptural injunction for lifelong [performance], how can there be an abandonment of the fires?", this will be examined in the section concerning the sequence of the four stages of life (*āśrama*).

(3) Others, however, say: the offering (*homa*) of village-grown foods is prohibited, but not their use for the sake of deities and so forth. But is it not the case that there is consumption even in that context, according to the rule: "The five, including the sacrificer, eat the *iḍā*"? True; but that is scriptural (*śāstrīya*), not worldly (*laukika*). And the prohibition [of village food] applies to the worldly kind, as in the verse: "Having completely renounced... (MDh 6.3). Furthermore, his entering the village for that purpose is not contradictory, for it will be stated later: "Or, having brought [food] from the village, he may eat" (MDh 6.28). This [objection] is incorrect, because of the injunction: "With the foods of sages" (MDh 6.5). Thus, everything beginning with "Having established the sacred fire according to the *Śrāvaṇika* [rite]" (GDh 3.27) is logically consistent.

For it is recited thus: "Having taken up the *agnihotra*," (MDh 6.4), but not "having abandoned it" (MDh 6.3). Furthermore, the ritual of reposing the fires (*samāropaṇa*) will be prescribed for one who is about to die or for one who has performed intense austerities during his first journey abroad. Nor is there any way to justify the application of terms such as *turāyaṇa* to the fires kindled in the month of Śrāvaṇa. The kindling of those fires by one whose wife has died shall be based on a specific scriptural injunction; or when one desires to go to the forest directly from the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*), then the kindling of the Śrāvaṇa fires applies. Therefore, the departure to the forest for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) must be accompanied by his wife and his fires.

And in that regard, the performance of Śrauta rites with rice and other grains must be carried out according to the prescribed rules. It must somehow be established that even rice and other such grains constitute the food of sages (*muni*). Rice and barley are also purifiers (*pavitra*). Furthermore, for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), the entrusting of his wife to the care of others may somehow find a place in the Smārta fire, since both [the Śrauta and Smārta fires] are of the nature of Smārta rites. Regarding the statement "having entrusted his second wife," this refers to a case where a man has two wives and the sacred fires have been led away by one of them. "Not neglecting" (*askandayan*): "neglect" (*skandana*) means the transgression of the rule, the failure to accomplish the performance as it has been prescribed. This [term] is for the purpose of completing the meter. The phrase "through application" (*yogataḥ*) is also [to be understood in this way]: "not neglecting through application" means not letting it perish through proper method (*yukti*). Method (*yukti*) is indeed the rule itself. (6.9)
One should perform the Darśeṣṭi, the Āgrayaṇa, and the Cāturmāsyas,
as well as the Turāyaṇa and the Dākṣāyaṇa in their proper sequence.

*Darśeṣi* and *āgrayaṇa* form a collective dvandva compound. The terms *cāturmāsya*, *turāyaṇa*, and *dākṣāyaṇa* denote specific Vedic ritual acts. For some, the *turāyaṇa* and other such rites are indeed obligatory (*nitya*). (6.10)
With pure foods fit for sages, gathered by himself during the spring and autumn seasons,
he should separately prepare the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) and the cooked oblations (caru) according to the prescribed rules.

When the phrase "with the food of sages" (*munyannaiḥ*) is not connected with what precedes, then there is no objection [to the question]: "How can the *vaitānika* rites, which are enjoined to be performed with rice and other grains, be carried out? In this context, the *caru* and *puroḍāśa* offerings are to be understood as those prescribed specifically in the *vaikhānasa-śāstra*. "Spring-grown" (*vāsantāni*) means those that are born or ripen in spring. Similarly, the phrase "with pure autumnal [grains]" is a restatement (*anuvāda*). [The term] "gathered by oneself" (*svayam āhṛtaiḥ*) excludes livelihoods such as receiving gifts (*pratigraha*) and so forth. The "taking away" (*apaharaṇa*) by means of repeated gathering (*punarhṛti*) and so on is for the purpose of performing the aforementioned *smārta* rituals. The words "according to rule" (*vidhivat*) and "separately" (*pṛthak*) serve as supplements to complete the sense. 6.11.
Having offered that most pure forest produce as an oblation to the deities, he should consume the remainder himself, along with salt prepared by his own hand. (6.12)

On the sacred festival days (*parvan*), one should consume only that which remains after being offered to the deities, and not vegetables, roots, fruits, and the like. One should apply the remainder to oneself—that is, utilize it for one's own sake, meaning for the maintenance of the body. Furthermore, one should not consume salt prepared by oneself, such as *saindhava* and other varieties. (6.12)
One should eat vegetables grown on land or in water, as well as flowers, roots, and fruits produced from pure trees, along with oils derived from fruits.
He may eat things grown on land and those born in water, as well as flowers, roots, and fruits. (6.13)
One should avoid honey, meat, mushrooms growing from the earth,
bhūstṛṇa grass, śigruka, and the fruits of the śleṣmātaka tree.

"Bhaumāni" means mushrooms. The word *kavaka* has been explained previously (*MDh* 5.19) as a synonym for the word *chatrāka*. These *kavakas* grow on the ground, but they also grow in tree hollows and similar places; therefore, the inclusion of the term "bhauma" (ground-born) is for the sake of specification. There is a contradiction with established practice, as mushrooms are prohibited without distinction among the duties of householders, yet an excessive restriction is appropriate for a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). Therefore, "bhaumāni" is an independent term. In this context, it should be understood as referring to a certain substance known among forest-dwellers called *gojihvikā*, and not to everything that merely grows from the earth. Since mushrooms are already prohibited, their repeated prohibition here is intended to establish that grasses growing from the earth (*bhūstṛṇa*) and the like require the same expiation. The words *bhūstṛṇa* and *śigruka* denote specific types of vegetables well-known among the Vāhikas. (6.14)
In the month of Āśvayuja, he should discard the food of sages previously stored, as well as worn-out garments, vegetables, roots, and fruits. (6.15)

Regarding the two positions of the six-month accumulation and the equal accumulation, the relinquishment occurs in the month of Āśvayuja. Now, one might object: the sage's food is accumulated only to the extent that it suffices for his ritual duties; there is nothing extra there. Of what, then, is there relinquishment? It is said: at the time of acquisition, it is not possible to weigh [the total]; therefore, whatever remains is relinquished in the month of Āśvayuja.
And indeed, worn-out garments; for those that are not worn out, there is no discarding. 6.15.
One should not eat what has been ploughed by a plow, even if it has been abandoned by someone; nor, even when distressed, should one eat flowers or fruits grown in a village. 6.16

There is a prohibition even against wild plants that have been ploughed. Village-grown plants, even those not produced by the plough, are prohibited by the rule: "having abandoned village food" (MDh 6.3). The meaning is that even when one is distressed and other options are unavailable, because the worship of deities and so forth must necessarily be performed, such items are not to be accepted even as substitutes. The word "api" (even) should be understood as displaced in its position: even flowers are not to be accepted, how much less grains? 6.16.
He may eat food cooked by fire, or he may eat only what is ripened by time;
he may be one who grinds with a stone, or even one who uses his teeth as a mortar.

That which is cooked by fire—such as vegetables, boiled rice, and so forth—is *agnipakva*; he who eats that is an *agnipakvāśana*. He should eat only what has been cooked by itself at the proper time, such as the fruit of trees; or else, having ground grains such as *nīvāra* and the like, this is his consumption. Having pounded them with stones—that is, with rocks—and reduced them to the form of flour, he should eat. Or else, whatever is produced by the season, such as gourds and the like, which have an outer husk or shell, he should remove that shell with stones and eat the inner fruit. One whose teeth serve as a mortar is a *dantolūkhalika*; having removed the husk-shell with his teeth, he should eat. Even in the absence of [other] preparation, he must not perform it [artificially]. Or rather, as before, it is a designation for a specific kind of food: he should eat such things that his teeth alone accomplish the function of the mortar, namely the threshing. (6.17)
He may be one who washes [his bowl] immediately after eating, or one who accumulates for a month; he may be one who stores for six months, or even one who stores for a year. (6.18)

Regarding that which was previously mentioned as "food" (*aśana*), he should acquire only enough for a single day’s meal. Alternatively, a "monthly accumulation" (*māsasaṃcaya*) refers to a store sufficient for a month; since he possesses such a store, the suffix *ṭhan* should be applied. Or else, the term *māsasaṃcayaka* should be understood here as a *bahuvrīhi* compound: "one who has a store sufficient for a month. The same applies to the two subsequent cases as well. (6.18)
One should eat food at night or by day, having procured it according to one's ability; or one may observe the practice of eating only every fourth mealtime, or even every eighth mealtime.

Since eating twice a day is prescribed for the sake of human necessity, the cessation [of one meal] at one of the two times is enjoined. Just as the age advances, so should one abandon the meal-time; one should resort even to the fourth [meal], making the eighth time the limit. Having passed three days and nights, one who eats in the evening on the fourth day becomes one who observes the eighth-meal rule (*aṣṭamakālika*). Because eating is the subject under discussion, it is understood that the connection with the fourth time refers specifically to that [act of eating]. (6.19)
Or he should pass through the bright and dark fortnights according to the rules for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
or else, at the ends of the two fortnights, he should eat boiled barley-gruel only once.
At the two ends of the fortnight—on the full moon day and the new moon day—one should eat the gruel prepared therein. "Once" means either in the evening or in the morning. 6.20.
Abiding by the doctrine of the Vaikhānasas, he should always subsist solely on flowers, roots, and fruits that have ripened in their own time and fallen naturally.

"Ripened by time": this is stated to exclude the cooking of jackfruit and similar fruits even by fire; such fire-cooked food is not forbidden for a householder. "Vaikhānasa" is the name of a scripture in which the duties of a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) are prescribed; he should abide by their tenets and also train himself in the other modes of conduct taught in that scripture. (6.21)
He should roll about on the ground or stand on his tiptoes for the duration of the day;
he should pass his time by standing and sitting, approaching water at the times of the three libations.

"Turning over" means sitting on one side on the bare ground and then remaining on the other side. One should conduct oneself in this manner, except for the times of eating and moving about; that is to say, one should not sit down, nor walk about, nor sit upon a bed, a seat, or against a wall. One should stand on the balls of the feet or on the tips of the toes. During the day, one should remain in these two postures—standing and sitting. However, regarding the night, he will later describe lying on the bare ground alone. Regarding the "approaching the waters" at the three libations—morning, midday, and afternoon—he indicates that when rivers and such are unavailable, bathing may be performed even with water drawn out [from a well]. (6.22)
In the summer he should practice the penance of the five fires; during the rains, he should live under the open sky;
and in the winter, he should wear wet clothes, thus gradually increasing his austerity.

One should torment oneself with five [fires]. Having placed fires in the four directions, one should stand in the middle and expose oneself to the heat of the sun from above. During the rainy season, one should take shelter in the open air under the clouds; in whatever place it rains, one should resort to that spot, and for the sake of warding off the rain, one should not take up an umbrella, clothing, or the like. In winter, this is for the purpose of characterizing the cold. By this, the same rule applies to the cool season as well: wearing wet clothes. Gradually, step by step. (6.23)
Performing ablutions at the three times of day, he should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
practicing most rigorous austerity, he should wither his own body.

"Sprinkling" (upasparśana) means bathing. Other forms of austerity (tapas) as well—such as keeping the arms raised, fasting for a month, or observing the twelve-night vow—he should emaciate his body by performing that which is more severe, more excellent, and productive of bodily pain. 6.24.
Having duly internalized the sacrificial fires within himself according to the prescribed rule,
he should become a sage without fire and without a fixed dwelling, subsisting on roots and fruits.

The *vaitāna* rites are those pertaining to the sacrificial canopy; that is, the Śrauta rituals. He should consign these into himself according to the procedure for consuming ashes and other such methods. The ritual for consignment into oneself is to be understood from the *Śravaṇaka*. When he has practiced austerity for a long time and has reached the seventy-year stage of life, then, while still a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), being without fires and without a fixed dwelling, he should abandon his leaf-hut intended for residence. Where, then, should he sit? As will be stated later: "having the root of a tree as his dwelling" (MDh 6.26). He should be a sage (*muni*). This is connected [with the previous verse]. By this, the following meaning is expressed: he should observe restraint of speech. One who maintains the vow of silence is called "one of restrained speech" in the world. He should subsist on roots and fruits. This is for the purpose of turning away from other food; he should not even eat wild grains (*nīvāra*) and the like found in the forest. (6.25)
Exerting no effort for the sake of pleasures, he was a celibate student who slept upon the ground;
having no sense of "mine" regarding shelters, his dwelling was at the foot of trees.

One should not exert effort toward objects that serve the purpose of pleasure; one oppressed by heat should not seek shade; one afflicted by cold should not kindle a fire. However, if the cessation of suffering from cold and the like occurs through the heat of the sun or other means provided by fate, such removal of suffering is not prohibited. This is prescribed for times other than the rainy season and so forth, because it is enjoined as a duty (*dharma*) for one who has undertaken [the practice].

Alternatively, if one is afflicted by disease, the application of medicine is forbidden; yet the cessation of disease is also called happiness. Therefore, one should not make an effort for its cessation.

One should sleep on the ground, lying upon a bare patch of earth covered only with grass. One should not form the notion of "mine" or attachment to dwellings—refuges such as houses, the roots of trees, and so forth. One should take the roots of trees as one's abode, serving the function of a home. In their absence, stone slabs, caves, and the like are also prescribed. (6.26)
He should obtain alms for his sustenance only from brahmins who are ascetics, or from other twice-born householders living in the forest. (6.27)

The locative case is used in the sense of the ablative. When fruits and roots are unavailable from ascetics, he should collect alms from householders, that is, from those living as forest-dwellers. "Sufficient for his journey" means just enough to satisfy him. 6.27.
But in the event of impossibility,
he who dwells in the forest may bring food from the village and eat eight morsels, having received them either in the hollow of his hand, in a leaf-cup, or in a potsherd. (6.28)

Because of the mention of "taking mouthfuls," this does not refer merely to begging for roots and fruits; rather, the consumption of village food is permitted by him when other [kinds of food] are unavailable. "Having taken" means with the hollowed palm itself, devoid of a vessel; "with a fragment" means with a broken piece of a shallow dish or similar object. 6.28.
A Brahmin living in the forest should practice these and other initiations, as well as various Upaniṣadic scriptures, for the sake of the perfection of the self. (6.29)

One should practice these initiatory observances (dīkṣā-niyamas) and others, such as standing within water or closing the eyes; one should study, reflect upon, and meditate on the Upaniṣadic scriptures—the Vedic statements recited in the section concerning the secret doctrine—for the sake of self-perfection. Or, various forms of meditation (upāsanā) have been taught for the purpose of attaining Brahman. The word "various" is a reiterative reference. 6.29.
These have been practiced by sages and brahmins, as well as by householders, for the sake of increasing knowledge and austerity and for the purification of the body. (6.30)

One should practice other [observances] as well, which have been mentioned without distinction. This prohibits even the practice of initiations such as those of the Śākyas and Pāśupatas, which would otherwise be implied. These [observances] are described in the *Mahābhārata* as having been practiced by the Ṛṣis when they were performing austerities and so forth, as well as by Brāhmaṇa householders. Thus it is said: "And this is not in conflict with those who follow the higher [path]" (GDh 3.10). One should increase—that is, strengthen—knowledge, which is the realization of the oneness of the Self, by studying the relevant scriptures. And for the purification of the body, one should observe rules regarding diet and initiatory rites. 6.30.
Or, having taken his stand upon the Aparājitā, he should proceed straight toward that direction,
disciplined and subsisting on water and air, until the fall of his body.

The intermediate direction between the east and the north is called Aparājita (the Unconquered) or Aiśānī (the Northern) among the worlds. Having taken his stand in that direction and fixed it in his mind, thinking, "This is the way I must go," he should then proceed along it. Moving straight and not walking crookedly, he should not avoid chasms or the currents of rivers. Until the fall of his body, he should remain disciplined, subsisting on water and air. This is the rule for proceeding toward the east and the north. As long as he does not fall, he should subsist on air and water; remaining disciplined (*yukta*), having yoked himself through the teachings of Yoga. This is what is called the Great Departure (*mahāprasthāna*). || 6.31 ||
Having cast off the body by means of any one of these practices of the great seers,
the Brahmin, freed from sorrow and fear, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.

The previously mentioned austerities (*tapas*) and the "Great Departure" (*mahāprasthāna*) just described constitute the conduct of the great seers (*maharṣicaryā*). By means of one of these, or by entering a river, falling from a cliff (*bhṛgu-prapatana*), entering fire, or abstaining from food, one should abandon the body. The fruit for such a person—whose grief and fear have departed—is the attainment of the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*). Grief is the experience of suffering in hell and other realms; fear is the thought, "I shall go to hell. These depart for him. Without any interval, and not by way of the sequence beginning with light (*arcir-ādi-krama*), he attains the world of Brahmā. Here, the "world of Brahmā" refers to a specific location that is superior even to heaven; there he is magnified, remaining in a state of being honored. However, he does not attain the sovereign rule of Brahman itself, because of the use of the term "world" (*loka*); for it is in the fourth stage of life (*āśrama*) that liberation (*mokṣa*) will be discussed.

They say that liberation is not produced by action alone. But has it not also been stated for this [path]: "And various Upaniṣadic scriptures for the sake of the perfection of the self" (MDh 6.29)? And the "perfection of the self" is the attainment of its state through the meditation upon the self; for no other meaning of the word *saṃsiddhi* is appropriate. In the Upaniṣadic scriptures, that which is to be realized—the self of the yogis—is described as: "Established in Brahman, he attains immortality" (ChU 2.23.1), and "Then he goes to union," and so forth (ChU 2.20.2).

Now, it may be argued: other perfections resulting from austerity (*tapas*) are also heard of in scripture, such as in the passage beginning, "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers" (ChU 8.2.1). Thus, for a person, there will be attainment of equal power (*sārṣṭitā*) and residence in the same world (*sālokya*) brought about by the fulfillment of his own resolve; however, this is not liberation (*mokṣa*). This is incorrect, because there is no distinction [between the two cases]. Just as one is qualified for meditations (*upāsanā*) that yield limited results, so too is one qualified for the attainment of immortality. Nowhere is it heard that meditations concerning non-duality must be performed exclusively by a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*).

But is it not the case that, having introduced the topic with "The three branches of dharma," the duties of the householder are stated by the passage "sacrifice, study, and charity"; the forest-dweller by "austerity alone"; the lifelong student by "the student who dwells in the teacher's family"; and the wandering mendicant by "one who is firmly established in Brahman"? For these three, worlds of merit are declared; therefore, by the principle of remainder, immortality belongs to one distinct from these.
It is not so. For this word "brahmasaṃstha" is used in its etymological sense (*yaugikatva*) to mean one who is established in Brahman and strives toward it with that as his sole aim.
Now, if all [orders of life] were entitled [to this], then it would have been sufficient merely to say, "One who is established in Brahman attains immortality" (ChU 2.23.1).

It is not so. While the fruits of the various orders of life (*āśrama*)—which are understood from their own respective injunctions—are subject to exhaustion and result in "meritorious worlds," for one who is established in Brahman while remaining in those very orders, immortality characterized by non-return is prescribed.

Now, it may be objected: the knowers of the Self maintain that Brahman is of the nature of non-duality (*advaita*), and that [state] is characterized by the cessation of action (*nivṛtta-karma*). The stages of life (*āśrama*) are called the path of engagement (*pravṛtta-mārga*), consisting essentially in the performance of actions, instruments, and their fruits. In that regard, there is a mutual contradiction between the realization of the non-dual Self and the duties of the householder and others, such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice, which depend upon the very distinctions [of agent, action, and fruit].

To this it is replied: This objection applies equally to the state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*), since restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) are also required; and these too depend upon distinctions.
Furthermore, it might be argued that for one who has renounced action and stands upon the path of cessation, there are no scriptural injunctions whatsoever.

This is not the meaning of the scripture. What will be taught as renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is simply the abandonment of the notions of "I" and "mine," not the abandonment of the entire purport of the scriptures. Even for such a person, when afflicted by hunger and the like, there certainly exists a relationship between action and its factors (*kriyā-kāraka-sambandha*) when they engage in begging and so forth. In that case, for one engaged in worldly activities whose purposes are visible, the cultivation of the knowledge of the non-dual Self is not contradictory; however, regarding scriptural duties such as the *agnihotra*, it would be contradictory—so who, being a reasonable person, could say such a thing?

Now it is said: even for one afflicted by hunger and the like, the abandonment of non-duality lasts only for that duration due to its opposing factor, namely eating. Just as for one walking in blinding darkness who steps upon a thorny place, once the sun has risen and light is regained, the traveler stands again rightly upon non-thorny ground; so too, when the affliction of hunger ceases—which serves as a momentary light—for one whose self-knowledge was interrupted, there is once more an abiding in non-duality alone by the power of firm latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

That is not contradictory even for an ascetic; for a householder as well, the practice [of meditation] by way of his sons, wife, and so forth, is not contradictory. However, for one who is occupied with many activities and has become habituated to duality, how can there arise the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of non-duality? And it is said regarding the duties of a householder: "He should reflect alone" (MDh 4.258), and likewise, "having entrusted everything to his son" (MDh 4.257).

But is it not the case that there is a scriptural text stating, "Therefore, one who desires heaven should not depart before the end of his lifespan" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.2.6.7)? In that case, how can there be the abandonment of the body by a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*)? For that scriptural text cannot be made applicable to anyone other than a forest-dweller by this Smṛti; for scripture is more authoritative, and it ought not to be restricted in accordance with a Smṛti.

It is said in reply: There is no contradiction with the scriptures for one who is about to die—whether due to being worn out by old age or because death is known to be imminent through the sight of undesirable omens and the like. For it is heard in the scripture: "Not before the end of one's lifespan. Indeed, if death were intended in an undesired state, the text would have simply said: "One desiring heaven should not depart [before then]. Furthermore, the teaching regarding the *ariṣṭas* (signs of approaching death) in the Upaniṣads becomes meaningful in this sense; however, for one whose death does not occur on account of such signs, [the rule remains as stated]. 6.32.
Having thus spent the third part of his life wandering in the forests, he should renounce all attachments and go forth as a wandering mendicant during the fourth part of his life. (6.33)

From this point forward, the intention is the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśrama*). Regarding the phrase "the third part": the meaning is that one should remain for some period of time. This refers to such a duration of time by which austerity (*tapas*) becomes well-performed and all desire for sense-objects (*viṣaya-abhilāṣa*) has ceased. Indeed, it is not possible to understand the "third part" here as referring strictly to a third portion of one's lifespan. For the stages of life (*āśramas*) do not depend upon a hundred-year lifespan; rather, the time for entering the third stage is stated to be upon the appearance of wrinkles, grey hair, and the birth of offspring. Furthermore, these do not necessarily arise for everyone at around fifty years of age. And it is stated elsewhere: "When austerity has reached perfection, one should renounce."

But surely, as in the case of other stages of life (*āśrama*), there is a defined time limit—brahmacarya ending with the completion of Vedic study, and the householder stage lasting until the appearance of wrinkles and grey hair—but here there is no such cause for limitation. If one were to rely on the literal text regarding the "third part [of life]," or the statement "when asceticism has reached perfection," even there a dependence on time is indeed appropriate; for it is not known by how much asceticism perfection is attained. Therefore, a temporal limitation is not fit to be stated.

It has been stated here that the determination of the third stage of life is not possible with reference to a lifespan of one hundred years. And the time has been specified: "One should enter the religious life when the body is mature. One should wander forth at such a time of austerity and such an age that an increase in intoxication is no longer to be feared. "Having lived" means having remained [in the householder stage] after performing the prescribed rule. Furthermore, the abandonment of attachments consists in relinquishing the sense of "mine," namely, delighting in solitude. (6.33)

Having gone from stage to stage of life, having offered oblations, having conquered his senses, and being weary from the practice of begging and making offerings, one who renounces the world prospers after death. (6.34)

This supports the position of cumulative practice. Regarding the phrase "from stage to stage": having gone from the householder stage to the forest-dweller stage, when one has offered the oblations and has conquered the senses in both stages, then one should go forth as a wandering mendicant. "He prospers after death" means that after dying, he attains a preeminent degree of splendor. "Exhausted for a long time by begging and the offering of oblations" refers to this restatement of the duties of the stages of life. (6.34)
Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation;
but he who pursues liberation without having discharged them goes downward. (6.35)

"Discharge" (apākaraṇa) means the complete clearing of debts. One should fix the mind on liberation (*mokṣa*). By the word "liberation," the stage of wandering mendicancy (*pravrajyā-āśrama*) is indicated. In that stage, it is said to have liberation as its sole primary fruit, whereas this is not the case for the other stages of life. Therefore, liberation is [identical with] the state of a wandering mendicant. 6.35.
What, then, are those three debts? To this he says:

"Having studied the Vedas according to the rule, having procreated sons in accordance with dharma, and having sacrificed with sacrifices according to one's ability, one should direct the mind toward liberation. (6.36)

"This person is born with three debts: to the gods by means of sacrifice, to the ancestors by means of progeny, and to the seers by means of Vedic study" (TS 6.3.10.5). This is a *smṛti* that restates what is declared in this *śruti*. Now, one might object: there is the *Jābāla-śruti*, which says, "Having become a householder, one should renounce; or else, otherwise, one may renounce even from the stage of the student (*brahmacarya*). To this it is replied: [the *smṛti*] cites that [scriptural passage] merely with reference to the fact of birth. However, in that context, this [other rule] is contradicted: "Likewise, without having procreated offspring... (MDh 6.37).

If this scriptural statement exists, then what [is the case]? This is said: "Because the householder stage is directly enjoined" (GDh 3.36). Regarding the word "one should go forth": for such a renunciant, there is no such thing as these specific rites being to be performed by him, or this particular procedure (*itikartavyatā*) to be followed. However, for the householder, the *agnihotra* and other rites are prescribed with all their constituent parts and subsidiaries; it is with this intention that [the sūtra] was stated. As for those lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika*) and others who, not having seen this scriptural passage, rely solely on the Smṛti—they are superseded by the householder stage through the direct injunction of the Śruti.

We do not understand the intention of those who describe the meaningfulness of the Smṛti texts on the grounds that they apply to those disqualified, such as the impotent and others. If it is argued that one is not entitled to Śrauta rites because of an incapacity for auxiliary acts such as gazing at the clarified butter (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*) or the Viṣṇu-steps (*viṣṇukrama*), since the injunctions regarding entitlement become meaningful only with respect to one capable of performing a rite endowed with such auxiliaries—and thus one who is incapable should not perform them—then by this same logic, how could the lame or the blind have an entitlement to the sequence of Smārta rites? For even among Smārta duties, there is the fetching of water-jars and so forth for the sake of the teacher by a lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*), and in the state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*), the rule "he should not stay in a village for a second night" (GDh 3.21). Furthermore, there is evidence for their initiation (*upanayana*); from that follows their request for marriage, as in "if there is a desire for a wife" (MDh 9.203). Even though initiation, the gaze at the sun, and the circumambulation of the fire are prescribed, and since marriage is impossible for one who has not been initiated due to his status as a *vrātya*, there remains the service to the teacher and even a deficient state of studentship (*brahmacarya*) to the extent possible. However, the impotent person, by his very nature, is simply not eligible for initiation; and he is not entitled to anything whatsoever, whether from his father or otherwise.

Therefore, the view that renunciation (*pārivrājya*) and lifelong studenthood (*naiṣṭhikatā*) concern those who are not qualified [for the householder stage] does not satisfy the mind. It is true that this will be like the censure of the fire-oblation performed at sunrise; the statement of censure, "without having discharged [the debts]" (MDh 6.35), is made by resorting to the position of cumulative performance (*samuccaya*), and is not an absolute prohibition. Alternatively, this should be understood as referring to the case where one whose marriage has not yet been contracted is entitled to renunciation. 6.36.
A twice-born man who, without having studied the Vedas, without having procreated offspring, and without having performed sacrifices, desires liberation, goes downward. (6.37)
Having performed the obligatory sacrifices with the consecrated fires, including those involving animals and Soma,
and having offered the Prājāpatya sacrifice in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee,
a Brāhmaṇa should consign the sacred fires into himself and depart from his home to lead a life of wandering mendicancy.

The *prājāpatya* sacrifice is prescribed in the *Adhvaryuveda*, and in that sacrifice, the giving away of all one's possessions (*sarvasvadāna*) is ordained. Having performed it, the sacred fires are consigned within oneself (*samāropyante*). The procedure for this consigning (*samāropaṇa*) is also to be understood from that very source. The compound *sārvavedasaṃ* functions as a bahuvrīhi, meaning "one whose sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of all the *veda*. Here, *veda* means wealth; all of that is to be given. The suffix *-a* is added here in its own sense (svārthika) after the word *prajñādi*, because that class is an open-ended group (*ākṛtigaṇa*).

Others, however, say that the *puruṣamedha* (human sacrifice) is a sacrifice dedicated to Prajāpati (*prājāpatyā iṣṭi*). In that rite, the first sacrificial animal is "a Brāhmaṇa for Brahmā," and since Brahmā is Prajāpati, and because designations proceed according to the primary [deity], the *puruṣamedha* is thus a sacrifice for Prajāpati. The giving away of all one's possessions (*sarvasvadāna*), the internalizing of the sacred fires (*agnisamāropaṇa*), and renunciation (*pravrajyā*) are prescribed in that very context. For thus says the Śruti there: "Then, having internalized the fires within himself, by means of that internalization, while awaiting the worship of the Sun, he should go toward the forest; at that very moment, he becomes firm with respect to gods and men."

As for the fact that she who has renounced the world after having deposited the fires within herself is designated by her wandering life as saying, "These very [fires] are my sacrifices," therefore, because of his death, they are given to her and become deposited within her own self. Consequently, in the case of the wife's death, there is renunciation, and not necessarily "the taking of another wife" (MDh 5.166); this is not so. Rather, it must be said that since it is recited in the text, "having given the fires to the wife, [one performs] the funeral rites," this is a human composition and not the Veda, such that we might criticize what was stated [therein]; this is the rebuttal. (6.38)
For him who, having granted fearlessness to all beings, goes forth from his home, there are worlds consisting of splendor, O teacher of Brahman. (6.39)

The praise of the fourth stage of life through the censure of the householder’s state: For in sacrifice animals are slain; and according to the view that "those possessing the nature of sprouting are sentient," the cutting of grasses and herbs constitutes a fear for living beings. It has been stated that this does not exist for one who has renounced the home and upon whom the sacred fires have been formally transferred. This is expressed by the words, "having granted freedom from fear to all beings. By this, he speaks of the non-acceptance of green grasses and leaves. They are full of splendor and eternally luminous; there, the rising and setting of the sun are no longer perceived. As it is said in the Upaniṣads, "From here upwards, the sun neither rises nor sets"—such are the words they speak. (6.39)
Since not even the slightest fear arises for the twice-born from living beings, there is no fear whatsoever for him once he is liberated from the body. (6.40)
This same point is stated again: the meaning is that for one who is liberated from the body, the present physical frame falls away. 6.40
Having gone forth from the household life, the sage, purified by his observances, should wander as a mendicant, indifferent even when sensual pleasures are presented to him. (6.41)

He should be devoted to and disciplined by purifying recitations of mantras, *darbha* grass, water-pots, and black antelope skins, or else by purifying penances (*kṛcchra*). A sage (*muni*) is one who speaks nothing at all. When desirable objects such as fine food and the like are brought before him by someone, or when sounds such as singing happen to be present by chance, or when his sons and others come into his presence, he should remain indifferent. He should not look upon these for long with an affectionate eye, nor listen to them, nor sit together with them. (6.41)

As it is said: "One should always wander alone for the sake of accomplishment, without a companion; seeing that what is accomplished belongs to the solitary one, he neither abandons [the path] nor is he abandoned. (6.42)

By this, delighting in solitude (*ekarāmatā*) is enjoined. By the phrase "all alone," the abandonment of former acquaintances is expressed. By the phrase "without companions," it is meant that one should not even accept former dependents and the like. For one who is completely free from attachment and aversion, equanimity toward all things arises in this way. Otherwise, when this very dependent stands near, the thought would arise: "This one is mine, but this one is not. This very attachment is the cause of limitation; for instance, as long as he remains, one thinks, "He belongs to me," and thus he is not abandoned by sons and others. Therefore, one is neither deprived of nor separated from sons and others, and does not experience the suffering of separation from them. Otherwise, there is great suffering in abandoning them again due to attachment. For him, no one dies, nor does he belong to anyone. (6.42)
He should be without fire and without a dwelling; he may resort to a village for the sake of food.
Indifferent, free from accumulation, the sage should be composed in his being. (6.43)

The prior absence of the *śrauta* fires has already been mentioned; by this [verse], the absence of the domestic fire (*gārhapatya*) is stated. Alternatively, this is a prohibition against cooking, as well as against fuel intended for the fire for the purpose of warding off cold and so forth. A *niketa* is a house. He may resort to a village for one night for the sake of food. Having accomplished his purpose, he should spend the remainder of his time in the forest. And this single night in the village is what was stated by Gautama (GDh 3.21). In that regard, if he is near the village, then his entry is solely for the sake of food; but if he is at a distance, then he may stay for one night. He should plan for the second night in the forest. An *upekṣaka* is one who is indifferent even toward insentient objects such as his water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*); he should not make them dependent on himself. Alternatively, he should not perform medical treatment for the body's ailments. Others, however, read "asaṃkasukaḥ. One who is unstable is a *saṃkasuka*; by the negation of that, he teaches steadfastness of mental disposition. A *muni* is one whose organ of speech is restrained. Being concentrated in his inner state (*bhāva*), that is, in his mind, he should avoid conceptual constructions with the intellect. He is concentrated by his inner state alone, and not by mere speech. 6.43.
A skull, the roots of trees, ragged clothing, solitude, and equanimity toward all things—these are the characteristics of one who is liberated. 6.44

The bowl for eating alms is a skull or a begging-bowl; the dwelling is at the roots of trees; the rags are pieces of coarse, worn-out cloth. Equanimity toward enemy, friend, and those who are neither, as well as toward oneself, is the characteristic of one who is liberated. It is said that liberation is not attained immediately; however, one does not become liberated merely by this much. 6.44
One should not rejoice in death, nor should one rejoice in life; one should simply await the time, just as a hired laborer awaits his wages. 6.45

By this, freedom from affliction is expressed: one should not desire death, nor should one seek life for the sake of attaining superior knowledge. One should simply await the time, thinking: "Whatever will come to pass, let it be so at that very time. Just as a laborer, having received his wages, awaits the appointed time, thinking, "I must perform this work for him today," and does not incur the loss of his pay if he stops prematurely; in the same way, liberation occurs through this method upon the fall of the body following the exhaustion of saṃsāra, and not by acting according to one's own whims. (6.45)
One should place one's foot down purified by sight; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak words purified by truth; and one should act with a mind that is purified. (6.46)

Having examined the path with his eyes, he should place his foot in such a spot where living beings do not suffer. Since it is already established that one should speak truthful speech, the inclusion of the word "purified" (*pūta*) indicates that the word "truthful" (*satya*) is intended as an illustration; by this, [the rule] becomes comprehensive. One should always be "purified in mind," meaning purified through the mind; one should not engage in coveting the property of others and so forth. (6.46)
One should endure harsh words and should not despise anyone;
nor, depending upon this body, should one harbor enmity toward anyone. (6.47)

Whatever one says by transgressing the scriptures is *ativāda*, which is unpleasant abuse. One should endure it, one should forgive it, and one should not abuse in return; nor should one become angry in the mind. Therefore, he will say: "When reviled, one should speak what is wholesome" (MDh 6.48). By this, the agitation of the mind is prevented; it is not a rule that one must utter the word "wholesome. For in that case, one would be a speaker of falsehood, saying one thing with the voice while thinking another in the heart. "One should not despise": one should not show contempt toward anyone. One should not overstep the honor due to teachers and others. Nor should one harbor enmity toward this body if someone should strike it. One should reflect: "What does it matter to me whether this body is destroyed or not destroyed? May my body consist of splendor (*tejas*). (6.47)
One should not respond with anger to one who is angry; when reviled, one should speak kindly;
and one should not utter false speech scattered through the seven gates. (6.48)

There are seven gates: the pairs *dharma* and *artha*, *dharma* and *kāma*, *artha* and *kāma*, *kāma* and *artha*, *kāma* and *dharma*, *artha* and *dharma*, and the *trivarga* (the three aims). One should not utter false speech concerning these subjects—that is, speech that is scattered or distracted among them. Because these are based on duality (*bheda*), and because all duality is unreal, it is called "false. What then? One should speak only that which is based on liberation (*mokṣa*). Alternatively, the seven vital breaths (*prāṇas*) in the head are the gates of speech.
Or else, there are the six sense organs with the intellect (*buddhi*) as the seventh; speech proceeds with respect to objects grasped by these.
Others say they have well-distinguished case endings. 6.48.
Delighting in the inner self, seated, indifferent, and free from worldly desires, one who seeks happiness should wander here with the self alone as his companion. (6.49)

One-pointedness that culminates in the attainment of the realization of the true nature of the self is "internal. One should remain intent on reflecting upon its meaning and finding delight therein. The phrase "without regard" is a restatement of what was said previously for the purpose of practicing [this state] apart from other objects and qualities. "Free from worldly bait" means free from desire; "bait" (*āmiṣa*) refers to meat, and by using this as an indicator for desire, the prohibition is established because living beings have an excessive longing for it. The rest has already been explained previously. (6.49)
He should never seek alms by means of portents or omens, nor by the science of astrology and bodily marks, nor by giving instructions or counsel. (6.50)

Portents—whether celestial, atmospheric, or terrestrial; eclipses, the rising of planets, the appearance of comets, fires in the quarters of the sky, earthquakes, and so forth—the fruit of these he should not proclaim out of a desire for alms. Omens include such things as the ill-fortune of a house. The science of constellations (*nakṣatra-vidyā*) includes such matters as "Today, Kṛttikā is suitable for work" or "Today is the constellation favorable for a journey. The science of bodily marks (*aṅga-vidyā*) consists of the characteristics of hand-writings and the like. Instruction (*anuśāsana*) concerns the king and his subjects: "One should conduct oneself in this manner," "There should be peace with this one and war with that one," "Why have you done this? or "Why do you not do this? Disputation (*vāda*) is the presentation of arguments and refutations when there is a disagreement regarding the meaning of a treatise, motivated by pride. (6.50)
One should not approach a house that is crowded with ascetics, Brahmins, birds, dogs, or other mendicants. (6.51)
"Thronged": he should avoid that place for the sake of alms where many people have gathered together to obtain food. (6.51)
With his hair, nails, and beard trimmed, carrying a bowl, a staff, and a water-pot,
he should wander constantly with self-restraint, not causing pain to any living beings.

He will describe the vessels. There are three staffs, for he is indeed a *tridaṇḍin*. *Kusumbha* refers to a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), not to safflower (*mahārajana*). The meaning of the second half of the following verse has already been established. 6.52.
His vessels should be non-metallic and free from cracks;
their purification with water is prescribed, just as for the *camasa* cups at a sacrifice.

The vessels for alms and for water should be non-metallic—that is, not made of gold or other metals—and free from cracks and holes. They should be rendered stainless by mere water, like the *camasa* cups; however, it should be understood that if a stain does occur, its removal must also be performed with another substance. 6.53.
A gourd, a wooden bowl, one made of clay, and likewise one made of split bamboo—
these, Svāyambhuva Manu declared, are the vessels for ascetics.
*Vaidala* refers to what is made from split bamboo and the like; these are the vessels for an ascetic, intended for alms and for water. (6.54)
One should go for alms at a single time; one should not seek after abundance. For a mendicant who becomes attached to alms also becomes attached to sense-objects. (6.55)

The rule that there should be only one mealtime is prescribed for the act of eating alms-food (*bhaikṣakārya*), and not for the act of wandering for alms itself. What is intended here is a prohibition against eating twice. In this context, having gone out once, one should not eat at a second time by setting aside a remnant; it is for that purpose that eating is prohibited. Therefore, he says: "One should not indulge in abundance. For it is through the desire for a second meal that abundance occurs. For one who finds delight in solitude, there should be no abundance of alms-food for the sake of dependents. By stating the reason, he prohibits even full satisfaction (*sauhitya*) while eating only once. (6.55)

When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle is laid aside, when the embers have gone out, when the people have finished their meal, and when the removal of the dishes has been completed—then a mendicant should always go for alms. (6.56)

The time when people have finished eating is "the time of those who have eaten" (*bhuktavajjana*). The same applies to "smokeless" (*vidhūma*) and the others. The "falling together of bowls" (*śarāvasaṃpāta*) is the discarding of the leftovers on the ground; when that has passed. By all this, he says that one should beg for alms at the time when the opportunity for giving alms during the first cooking period has ceased. By the words "smokeless," etc., he indicates the commencement of the second cooking. "The mortars are set down" means they have been placed aside, having ceased from the act of pounding. (6.56)

One should not be despondent in the absence of gain, nor should one rejoice in its presence. One should possess only what is necessary for the maintenance of life, having emerged from attachment to material requisites. (6.57)

If, at such a time, nothing is obtained from anywhere, then one should not succumb to dejection or mental distress. One should not harbor joy or sorrow regarding gain or loss. "The measure for the sake of sustaining life" refers to the quantity of alms-food. By this he shows that in the event of a lack of alms, the maintenance of life may be carried out even with fruits, roots, water, and so forth, provided they are unclaimed. "Measure" (*mātrā*) also refers to the bowl, staff, and other requisites; "withdrawn from attachment" means having turned away from the effort to acquire them—that is, being free from desire. (6.57)
One should, however, utterly loathe gains obtained through honor;
for even an ascetic who is already liberated becomes bound by gains obtained through honor. (6.58)

That which one gives after having honored [the recipient] is "gain from the honored"; one should "despise" that—meaning one should censure or condemn it—and for this reason, one should not practice what is censured at any time, "in every way. One should not accept such alms even for a single day. The subsequent portion is an explanatory praise (arthavāda): for there is no possibility of bondage for one who is already liberated. (6.58)
By consuming little food and by staying and sitting in solitude, one should withdraw the senses that are being carried away by the objects of the senses. 6.59
A secluded place is one devoid of people; there, standing and sitting should be performed. By this, the conquest of the senses as the fruit of delighting in solitude is demonstrated.
Alternatively, freedom from curiosity is expressed by this: one should not remain even for a moment where many crowds of people consisting of men and women are seen with various ornaments. (6.59)
Through the restraint of the senses, through the destruction of passion and hatred, and through non-violence toward living beings, one becomes fit for immortality. (6.60)

Cessation is the obstruction of the activity directed toward its own object. "It conduces to immortality" means it becomes capable of, or fit for, immortality. This shows that this [cessation] is just like the knowledge of the Self. 6.60
One should contemplate the destinies of men arising from the defects of their actions, as well as their falling into hell and the torments in the abode of Yama. (6.61)

This analytical contemplation on the ultimate truth is called the investigation into the true nature of saṃsāra, which is essentially suffering. How indeed might this person transform the bodily affliction of wandering forth, the practice of mendicancy, and so forth—which are causes of suffering due to the abandonment of friends, kinsmen, children, wife, wealth, and power—into something that is performed without flaw, whether through necessity or by one's own free will? The destinies of human beings abound in suffering; they arise from the defects of karma resulting from the practice of prohibited acts, such as violence, theft, adultery, harshness of speech, calumny, and evil intentions. Even in this very world of living beings, there are destinies such as poverty, disease, humiliation, or physical deformity, as well as the experience of their consequences. In the hereafter, there is the falling into hellish pits, birth as worms or insects in impure places filled with urine and excrement, and the tortures in the abode of Yama, such as being boiled in cauldrons. (6.61)
Likewise, this other [truth] must be considered: separation from loved ones and union with those who are not loved, being overcome by old age, and being tormented by diseases. (6.62)

The accusative case is used because of the presence of the verbal action "one should observe" (*avekṣeta*). "Dear ones" refers to sons and other kinsmen; "separation from them" means being parted from those who have died before their time. "Union with the unpleasant" refers to encounters with enemies through battle and the like. Regarding "old age": old age is a particular state in the fourth stage of life; its "overpowering" consists of the destruction of the body's form, incapacity, impairment of the sense faculties, an abundance of diseases such as cough and asthma, being undesirable to all, and being an object of ridicule—these and similar factors constitute the overpowering by old age. Furthermore, for some, there is the affliction by diseases even prior to old age. (6.62)

Yet, even for one situated thus, great thirst persists. In that case, this [thirst] arises as an incurable affliction even against one's will. It brings about the departure from the body and again the conception in a womb—the wanderings of this inner self through thousands of millions of births. (6.63)

The departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) is an internal severance, and that pain is unbearable. Furthermore, there is birth in the womb; therein lies manifold suffering due to the non-emergence of the sense organs, a state of darkness for one dwelling in the belly, and the pain described by physicians arising from the mother’s food—whether it be excessively cold or hot, or deficient or excessive in measure. For the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), there are traversals through thousands of millions of wombs, reaching the paths of animals, hungry ghosts, worms, insects, moths, dogs, and so forth.

But surely, the inner self is held to be all-pervading and eternal; for that which pervades the entire world, how could there be an exit, and where could there be a departure from the womb? Furthermore, birth within a womb is impossible for that which is eternal.

It is said: There is a certain view according to which this person (*puruṣa*), the size of a thumb, resides within the body; consisting of the subtle elements, mind, intellect, and ego, he follows the course of *dharma* as long as *saṃsāra* lasts, and when that [dharma] has been accumulated, the power of consciousness (*caitanya-śakti*) becomes manifest. Therefore, the attributes of that [dharma] are figuratively attributed to the inner self (*antarātman*). Alternatively, it is said that "he departs" when those vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, which have their being in him, depart. In the same way, his "origination" (*saṃbhava*) is also to be understood.
Furthermore, we shall explain this again in the twelfth [chapter]. What need is there for more? 6.63
And [he understands] the connection with suffering for embodied beings arising from unrighteousness, as well as the imperishable union with happiness arising from righteousness and purpose. 6.64

From *adharma* comes "origination," that is, birth. "Union with suffering" is the experience of pain. From *dharma*, which is a category defined by the aforementioned characteristics, comes union with inexhaustible happiness. This too must be considered; the intention is that the life of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*) is the primary *dharma*. (6.64)
And by means of yoga, he should contemplate the subtlety of the Supreme Self, as well as its manifestation within bodies, both high and low. (6.65)

Yoga is the steadiness of the fluctuations of the mind, as demonstrated by Patañjali (cf. YSū 1.2). By means of that, one should investigate the subtlety of the Self, the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*). One should not form the notion of "Self" with respect to the body and so forth, or the vital breaths and so forth; rather, the intent of this is that through the excellence of knowledge born of yoga, one must understand [the Self] as distinct from all these internal and external principles. For there are no such conceptual constructs as "grossness" and so on belonging to the Self. And just as its birth occurs in the bodies of superior beings such as gods, and the experience of results occurs through its presiding over the body even though it is omnipresent, so too does it occur in inferior states among animals, *preta*s, *piśāca*s, and so forth. On the view of monism, the established position is that the Knowers of the Field are indeed the manifestations of the Supreme Self. Therefore, it is said that one should investigate the courses of the Supreme Self. 6.65
Even if adorned, one should practice the Dharma, devoted to whichever stage of life one finds pleasure in;
being equal toward all beings, the external mark is not the cause of righteousness.

Adorned with ornaments such as flowers and bracelets, the religious duty (*dharma*) of the wandering mendicant is that which has been prescribed for him, such as the meditation upon the Self (*ātmopāsana*); he should perform that with diligence. Whichever stage of life (*āśrama*) he belongs to, he should practice what is ordained for that stage. He should not consider himself a true ascetic (*yati*) merely by wearing the external marks such as the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*); rather, he should be equal toward all beings. The essential meaning is that he should diligently avoid passion, hatred, and greed. This does not mean that the wearing of ornaments is permitted simply by the abandonment of the [ascetic] marks. (6.66)
Although the fruit of the *kataka* tree clarifies water, the water does not become clear merely by uttering its name. (6.67)

When turbid water has the fruit of the *kataka* tree cast into it, it becomes clear and attains a state of pure transparency; however, that water does not become purified merely by the mention of the name of that fruit. Rather, it requires actual application. In the same way, the wearing of the sectarian mark (*liṅgadhāraṇa*) stands in the place of the name of the fruit. Accomplishment does not come from that alone, so long as the practice of dwelling in solitude, meditative worship, equanimity toward all things, and other such duties have not been performed. This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) supplementary to what precedes. (6.67)
For the sake of protecting living beings, whether by night or by day, he should always walk upon the earth after carefully scanning it, even when his body is in distress. (6.68)

Regarding what was stated, "One should place [the foot] purified by sight" (MDh 6.46), this verse demonstrates its purpose: even when the body is in distress—that is, even when there is bodily pain—whether by night or by day, one must not, without having looked, allow the body to come into contact with grass spread out for the purpose of lying down. There is an expiation for this transgression. Alternatively, this is intended for the sake of certain extremely minute small creatures which perish merely by the compression of the various parts of the body. 6.68.
Whatever living beings a wandering ascetic unintentionally injures by day or by night,
for the sake of their purification he should bathe and perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
"Living beings" should be understood as "small creatures. The connection is that [the practice is for] the purification of whatever sin exists in the harming of them. (6.69)
Even three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) performed according to rule by a Brāhmaṇa,
joined with the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava, should be known as the highest austerity.

By the word *brāhmaṇa*, he states that this is a duty pertaining to the [entire] caste (*jāti*); this rule does not apply to the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) alone, but to all three [classes]. Beyond these three, there is an increase in the fruit; however, these three must necessarily be performed. The *vyāhṛtis* are those mentioned in the verse, "preceded by the syllable *oṃ*" (MDh 2.81). The *praṇava* is the syllable *oṃ*. They are joined with these. At the time of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), this should be meditated upon. These are of three kinds, known as *kumbhaka*, *recaka*, and *pūraka*. Among them, *kumbhaka* and *pūraka* consist in the restraint of the exit of the primary nasal air; *recaka* occurs through the continuous expulsion of air from without without inhaling. The limit [of duration] is shown in the second chapter: "or else, by means of austerity, for as long a time as no pain arises. (6.70)
Just as the impurities of metallic ores are burned away when they are being smelted, so too are the defects of the senses consumed by the restraint of the vital breath. (6.71)

The *dhātus* are gold and other such minerals; when they are smelted, only the gold remains. Likewise, when the senses perceive their objects, joy and distress arise; the burning away (*dāha*) of the sin associated with those two occurs through the restraint of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). The arising of joy and distress is forbidden for one seeking liberation. However, even for an embodied being who has abandoned attachment and whose senses are controlled, these may still arise to some degree by the inherent power of things when forms, sounds, and so forth are encountered by chance. Therefore, breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) is for the purpose of removing that defect. (6.71)

One should burn away defects by means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and sin by means of concentrations (dhāraṇā); one should burn away attachments by means of withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and ungodly qualities by means of meditation (dhyāna). 6.72.
That [the mind is purified] "by means of breath-restraints" has been shown by the preceding verse.
Others, however, say: the defects are passion and so forth; one should burn them away.

How can these [passions] be burned by breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*)? It is logical that sin is burned by them; for its arising is imperceptible, as defined by the scriptures, and its cessation likewise. However, passion and the rest are objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, the relationship between the object to be removed and the remover in their case ought to be known through perception and so forth, not through scripture. If the scripture were to say, "One should remove that which has the nature of desisting," what would be its authority? Consequently, unwholesome conduct caused by passion and the like is designated by the word "defect" (*doṣa*). Its "burning" consists in the burning of its effects; for in their own nature, actions perish by their very essence due to their momentariness.
