This alone is "burning," and not, as in other cases, the state of being reduced to ashes. And thus, this is a restatement of the meaning of the preceding verse.

And by means of *dhāraṇās*. Now, is it not the case that *kilbiṣa* is sin (*pāpa*) and that it is the same as *doṣa*? In that case, one should have said simply: "One should burn away defects (*doṣas*) by means of breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāmas*) and *dhāraṇās*. What is the purpose of the word *kilbiṣa*? Or let there be the word *kilbiṣa*; what is the use of including the word *doṣa*? It is said in reply: The inclusion of the word *doṣa* must necessarily be made so that it may be understood that the burning away of specific sins occurs through breath-restraints, and not of every [sin]. For by the word *doṣa*, passion (*rāga*) and the like are denoted; therefore, the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) to sin, which is caused by those [defects], is as has been stated.
If that is so, then let that very thing be done; what is the point of this word "kilbiṣam" (sin)?

There is no fault here, as it is for the purpose of completing the meter. In that regard, breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) are said to be the burners of sin already arisen, whereas the concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) prevent the arising of faults altogether. But what, then, are these concentrations?

By means of tranquility (*śama*), self-restraint (*dama*), and other such practices, the mind—which is being drawn away by the desire to perceive sense objects—is held steady and restrained in that very place [of meditation]. And those reflections on the defects inherent in sense objects are such as "the skeleton-pillared [city]" (*MDh* 6.76), and so forth. The luster, charm, youth, physical form, valor, and other qualities seen in women are the causes of desire; these are grasped through conceptual perception (*savikalpa-pratyakṣa*). And conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) are streams of the mind. Therefore, by means of other conceptualizations—such as "this body is filled with urine and excrement" regarding that reflection on the defects in the object; "this so-called female substance is merely a collection of bones and rags"; "that which living beings desire from of old is actually something they ought to avoid"; "even this delusion of a fragment of pleasure is momentary, and its indulgence leads to terrible and long-lasting torments of Yama"—these [desires] can be restrained. This very process is called *tatprasaṃkhyāna*. In the same way, one should reflect upon food and other such things: "Whether it be this sugar, clarified butter, *pūra*, fresh butter (*haiyaṅgavīna*), milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and so on, or alms-food consisting of coarse grain and the like, there is no difference between them insofar as they serve to sustain the body. Any distinction that might appear as a specific quality for someone present for only a mere moment on the tip of the tongue is a momentary appearance resembling a city of Gandharvas. In this manner, he instructs that one should likewise reflect upon the defects in touch and other sensations.

Others, however, say: *dhāraṇā* is the retention, by the power of practice, of the abdominal air as it moves through the mouth and nose within the space of the heart, which is a specific part of the body.
But one might ask: what is the difference between these [practices] and the common *prāṇāyāmas*?

The distinction is that *dhāraṇā* consists of holding [the breath] at will even in places such as the arms or the forehead, without the meditation on the *vyāhṛtis* and so forth; whereas *prāṇāyāmas* are governed by exhalation (*recana*).
Others, however, maintain that "friendliness, joy, compassion, and equanimity—these are the concentrations" (cf. YSū 1.33).
Friendliness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, when established toward all living beings, quickly lead the meditator to the world of Brahmā; these indeed are the concentrations.

In this context, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the absence of hatred, but not affection for a friend, because that has the nature of bondage. Compassion (*kṛpā* or *karuṇā*) is a mental quality (*cittadharma*); it is the desire to rescue, upon seeing suffering beings, thinking, "How might this person be lifted out of this suffering? It has been stated that it is not merely the non-commencement of harm or the granting of favor. Therefore, it is said thus: this mental quality is to be practiced. Sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is the turning away from sorrow, whether caused by illness and so forth, or by the fear of hell and so forth; it is not, however, exhilaration, because that is a cause of passion (*rāga*). Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is well known in relation to objects, toward those who help, and toward those who cause harm.
*Dhāraṇā* (concentration) is the steadiness of the mind within the space of the heart through devotion to the contemplation of Brahman.

*Pratyāhāra* (withdrawal) burns away *saṃsarga*—the connection of the senses with their objects, which is their engagement therein. This is achieved either by the withdrawal of the senses from that [engagement] or by creating an obstruction to it. When confronted with a wondrous form, such as a bracelet or the sight of a beautiful woman, one should close the eyes or direct the gaze elsewhere; the same applies to all the senses. In this way, the yogi’s meditative absorption (*samādhi*) becomes unobstructed.

By means of meditation, one should burn away the non-sovereign qualities—namely, the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. These qualities are non-sovereign, dependent, and their forms are subject to consciousness. The conceit of the unchanging *puruṣa*—who is devoid of pleasure and the like—that "I am happy," "I am miserable," which is the conceit of identity with the qualities despite being devoid of them, must be burned away by meditation on the discrimination between the qualities and the *puruṣa*. One should thus practice the discrimination between the qualities and the *puruṣa*, thinking: "The *puruṣa* is of the nature of consciousness and devoid of qualities; *prakṛti* consists of the qualities. (6.72)
How is that to be performed? And what, moreover, is to be meditated upon by means of meditation? To this he says:
"Through the yoga of meditation, one should perceive the course of this inner self among beings high and low—a course difficult to be known by those of unrefined soul. (6.73)

The inner self (*antarātman*), the inner controller (*antaryāmī*), is the Person (*puruṣa*); its course, that is, its true nature, must be understood as it really is. The conceit of pleasure and pain is not limited to human birth alone; rather, the notion of "I" and "mine" regarding various high and low beings—such as animals, ghosts, and spirits—is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*) and must be removed.

Alternatively, one should reflect: "How is it that this omnipresent Self, who is greater than the intermediate space, greater than heaven, greater than these worlds—possessing all desires, all tastes, all smells, and all touches—is made dependent by actions upon such a body, which is subject to hunger and thirst and experiences pleasure and pain only partially through its various bodies? Alas, what power do actions have! This Self, who is the soul of all and independent, is rendered subservient by actions. I shall no longer perform these actions, which stand in the place of a wicked master; like a hired servant, I shall merely attend to them. Just as a certain servant, having entered service to please his master out of necessity, might think: "As long as he remains so difficult to approach, prone to punishment, intent on threats, and harsh in speech, I will not serve him further; I shall simply repay with labor whatever wages or the like I have received from him," so should one remain reflecting. One should meditate thus: "I shall reach the end of performed actions by experiencing their fruits, and I shall not perform others. Likewise, having determined through the study of the Vedānta and other means: "Are these individual souls (kṣetrajñas) manifestations of the Supreme Self, or are they independent? No, there is nothing whatsoever other than the Supreme Self," one should meditate accordingly.

Others, however, say: *dhyānayoga* means meditation (*dhyāna*) and yoga (*yoga*). By means of that, one should perceive the course of the inner self; having examined it, one should remain seated, perceiving the course through both meditation and yoga.

Alternatively, yoga is for the sake of meditation—that is, the steadiness of the mind—and having achieved that, one should perceive the course of the self. Through meditative practices, one should bring face-to-face the stainless form described in the Vedāntas, which is distinguished by qualities such as being free from decay and immortal.
It cannot be known by those whose selves are "unmade" (*akṛta*), meaning unrefined by the scriptures. (6.73)
One endowed with right vision is not bound by actions;
but one devoid of vision enters the cycle of transmigration. (6.74)

He states the result of the immediately preceding injunction: "One endowed with right vision"—that is, one who has attained the direct realization of the self as it truly is—“is not bound by actions” and “does not follow the cycle of rebirth,” because the actions already performed are exhausted through experience and no further actions are undertaken. However, by this it is not meant that liberation arises from knowledge alone; for one who is devoid of the internal vision taught in the Vedānta and performs only ritual actions, he enters the cycle of rebirth. (6.74)
By means of non-violence, detachment from the senses, Vedic rites, and the practice of severe austerities, they attain that state in this world.

However, these two verses serve as evidence that liberation results from the combination of knowledge and action: knowledge was explained by the preceding [verse], while by this [pair of verses] actions are now described.

Which, then, are the Vedic rites whose fruit is the attainment of that state? It is said: those which are performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), the fruits of which—such as heaven and so forth—are explicitly heard within their own injunctive statements (*vidhi-vākya*). To postulate another fruit beyond that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), or it would render the assumption of a mixed fruit purposeless. Furthermore, since the meaning of the sentence is completed by that much, how could there be a connection with a fruit characterized by the attainment of that state, which is not required by the injunction? When the purpose of the injunction is fulfilled through a syntactically connected element that is actually heard in the text, the injunction does not require anything else.

To this it is replied: There is indeed another statement here, namely, "He attains that through sacrifice," in the section concerning the secret doctrines (*rahasya*). Consequently, due to the principle of the distinctness of connection (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), two results are appropriate. Therefore, for all optional rites (*kāmya*), there will be no contradiction between their connection with uninterrupted results and their purpose of attaining the supreme state. In that regard, through the two sacrifices performed as distinct applications, both heaven and liberation (*apavarga*) arise. Furthermore, no specific sacrifice is heard of here by which this result would belong only to the obligatory rites (*nitya*) and not to the optional ones.

Now, it might be argued: since the delimitation of a fruit is not heard of in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), there is no contradiction [in their being the object], and thus it is logical that [the statement] refers to them, but not to optional rites (*kāmya*). For by that much alone, the phrase "by that sacrifice" (*tāvataiva yajñena*) attains universal applicability. If this is said:

What is the use of hearing about a fruit in this context? Vedic sentences culminate in what is to be done (*kartavyatā*). And that duty is understood through words such as *yāvajjīvam* (as long as one lives), even without a Vedic word for a fruit. Even there, a connection with a fruit is not required at all; if it were to be postulated, it would be redundant and thus could not achieve the same purpose. Therefore, the sentence "by sacrifice" (*yajñena*), finding no other basis, refers to the distinct domain of everything denoted by the word "sacrifice," both obligatory and optional.

And this is not the fruit of optional rites (*kāmya*), because it is not heard [in scripture] that one desires liberation (*apavarga*). It was with this very intention that it was stated: "Being motivated by desire is not praised" (MDh 2.2). In the *Mahābhārata* as well, it says: "Let not the fruit of action be your motive, nor let there be attachment to inaction" (BhG 2.47).

Therefore, for one whose internal organ is enveloped by the grasping at difference, who possesses craving and ignorance, and who is not liberated from the notions of "I" and "mine," there is the attainment of a limited fruit intended toward a specific goal. For the other, however, because he is impelled by no particular fruit but acts with the understanding that "this must be done," there is the attainment of Brahman, which consists of immeasurable and unsurpassed bliss.

Nor should this be objected to: "Since it is impossible to perform all one hundred and seven sacrifices, or however many there may be, would this not result in an instruction for non-commencement? For here, the perfection of performance is achieved through the perfection of vision alone. Therefore it has been said: "One who is endowed with right vision" (MDh 6.74). And all sacrifices are to be accomplished through vision. Thus it has also been said: "Other Brahmins worship by means of knowledge alone" (MDh 4.24).

Alternatively, the phrase "to whatever worlds one goes" is an indication by way of limitation, such as "one who desires heaven" or "one who desires a son. Those whose inner selves are permeated by the grasping of distinctions regarding the past and so forth proceed toward the primary human goal through mere untruth, out of greed for visible results. As some say: just as a child is induced to take medicine for the sake of nourishment by the false promise, "Your crest-lock will grow," so too do they proceed.

There is another opinion: here, "rites" (*karmāṇi*) are intended to mean the obligatory rites (*nityakarma*). These, when not performed, act as obstacles because they are causes of transgression (*pratyavāya*). Therefore, when these are performed, since the obstacle is absent, it is said [in the verse] "and by Vedic rites. Even though those rites are not enjoined for the sake of liberation, [by performing them] they "accomplish"—that is, they secure—the "place," meaning the station or the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*), of that Brahman; [places] that are "fierce," being extreme causes of bodily torment.
Alternatively, "his state" (tadīyapadam) refers to the nature of his authority—namely, universal sovereignty, autonomy, and the attainment of that very form. || 6.75 ||
It has bones for its pillars, is bound together by tendons, plastered with flesh and blood, covered with skin, foul-smelling, and filled with urine and excrement. (6.76)

This is for the purpose of generating dispassion. Let alone the bodies of worms, insects, moths, and the like, or those born from water, mud, or sweat; even this human body, which is held in high regard as something desirable—this very thing of which humans are perpetually afraid and fearful of falling—is like a small hut made of urine and excrement. Now he describes that little hut: the bones are like pillars, supported by them; bound together by sinews; smeared on the outside with flesh and blood as a plaster; and covered on top by the skin of the body—or rather, concealed above that. It is full of urine and excrement; the genitive case here is used in the sense of "full of," as in the expression "full of rice. (6.76)
One should abandon this abode of the elements, which is possessed by old age and sorrow, a dwelling place for disease, afflicted, full of passion, and impermanent. (6.77)

Old age is a particular state in the final stage of life, the cause of the body’s deterioration. It is afflicted, being constantly seized by diseases. It is full of passion, yearning for all objects; and when these are not obtained, it brings great suffering that must be endured through everything, being incurable and irreversible. Therefore, having considered this, one should abandon this body. It is the dwelling place of the elements—the transformations of the earth element—namely fat, marrow, phlegm, urine, semen, and blood; for they dwell here, but this is not the dwelling of the Self, because the Self is omnipresent. Therefore, one should not harbor craving for the body. (6.77)
Just as a tree leaves the riverbank, or as a bird leaves a tree, so too, by abandoning this body, one is liberated from the crocodile of suffering. 6.78

Regarding this body, which is like a small hut, its analogies are the riverbank and the tree. It should not be abandoned by one’s own will through such means as entering fire; rather, one should not form an attachment (*tṛṣṇā*) toward it. Its eventual falling away will occur spontaneously through the exhaustion of karma, just like that of a tree standing on a riverbank. As it is said: "One should not rejoice in death" (MDh 6.45). However, he who has attained the light [of knowledge], who has mastered the movement of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and whose mind is restrained from the transformations of delusion—he should effect his departure beforehand, just as a bird leaves a tree. The term *grāha* is used here because, like a crocodile, it is similar in being a cause of suffering. Thus it is said: even for one who has previously attained [the goal] with great difficulty, as long as the body exists, suffering inevitably persists due to the inherent nature of things. This is stated in response to a prior misconception. (6.78)
Having cast off his good deeds toward those dear to him and his evil deeds toward those who are not dear, through the yoga of meditation, he attains the eternal Brahman. (6.79)

The agitation of the mind caused by joy and distress, characterized by elation, grief, and so forth, must be avoided by this means: one should reflect and meditate upon the mind with the following reasoning: "Whatever pleasant thing someone does for me is distinguished as a result of my own past merit; this agent does not do what is pleasant out of affection for me, nor can he inflict upon me the enmity of evil deeds that cause suffering. By reflecting thus, one should cultivate this in the mind through the yoga of meditation. Consequently, neither attachment toward one who does what is pleasing nor hatred toward one who does what is unpleasing arises in him. Acting in this way, he approaches—that is, attains—the eternal and perpetual Brahman; he is not obstructed by the path beginning with light (*arcis*). From the inclusion of the term "eternal," non-return is understood. (6.79)
When one becomes free from longing for all things through one's inner disposition, then one attains eternal happiness both in this world and after death. (6.80)

This is an instruction regarding the nature of the mind (*citta-dharma*). One should not cultivate longing for desired objects by abandoning their acquisition; rather, one should abandon the cause of that longing. "Bhāva" refers to a mental state (*citta-dharma*) or a characteristic of desire belonging to the self. [The phrase applies] to all things (*sarva-bhāveṣu*). The second word, *bhāva*, signifies "entities" or "objects. By the inclusion of the term "all," attachment—even toward drinking, eating, and so forth, which are necessary causes for the maintenance of the body—is prohibited; however, mere desire (*icchā*) is not. For that [desire] arises naturally from the capacity of the object itself, such as hunger and thirst. Furthermore, desire (*icchā*) is distinct from longing (*spṛhā*): longing is bound up with passion (*rāga*) and has dejection as its cause; desire, however, arises spontaneously in relation to food and drink immediately following the digestion of what has been eaten and drunk. (6.80)
By this method, having gradually abandoned all attachments, one who is completely liberated from all dualities abides in Brahman alone. (6.81)

Having abandoned all attachments—attachment being the notion "this is mine" regarding cows, horses, elephants, gold, slaves, wives, fields, dwellings, and so forth—by relinquishing those and by embracing delight in solitude, one abides in Brahman, which is the nature of consciousness, having primarily resorted to this [state] first; then, by means of this aforementioned method consisting of the performance of external and internal ritual acts, actions do not bind him. He becomes liberated from all dualities, such as pleasure and pain, which arise from auspicious and inauspicious actions. (6.81)
All this that has been described here is indeed meditative;
for no one who is not a knower of the inner self ever enjoys the fruit of ritual action.

When there is meditation (*dhyāna*), that which pertains to meditation arises; it is obtained while one is practicing meditation. What is this? It is that which has just been declared and spoken of directly (*ābhimukhyena*), though not yet fully established through its underlying purpose (*tātparya*). This is the assignment of the fact that good and evil deeds are the causes of the pleasant and the unpleasant for a person. That a person acts unpleasantly is like a fever being a cause of pain, or like fire having the nature of burning when approached improperly. Just as one who is burned by fire does not hate the fire, so too should one regard even a person who acts unpleasantly; one should not seek to prevent them. And this occurs when there is meditation—that is, when the mind is one-pointed. At all times, this must be cultivated in the heart: that pleasure and pain are the fruits of action. The king is not the giver of happiness, such as a village and the like; rather, the acquisition of these upon first approaching him is due to my own exertion. Previous meritorious action is the giver, not the king. Likewise, the staff is not the tormentor; it is actions that torment me, not the king, nor is anyone else capable of doing so. All of this should always be meditated upon and reflected upon. Furthermore, that which was said to generate detachment from worldly existence—beginning with "the skeleton-pillared [body]" (MDh 6.76)—that too must be constantly contemplated.
For one who does not know the inner self [is not qualified].

(1) Here, "inner mind" (*adhyātma-citta*) is what is being discussed. When one does not understand this which has been thus proclaimed, does not ascertain it, and does not cultivate it through practice, one does not enjoy the fruit of action. For a wandering mendicant, there is the act of begging for alms, dwelling for a single night in a village, and so forth; yet he does not obtain its fruit, which is called liberation. This means that as long as a state of desirelessness toward everything has not arisen through the cultivation of [meditations on] the skeleton-pillar and so forth, and as long as the abandonment of passion and hatred has not been achieved by consigning the fruits of actions [to the Lord], [the goal is not reached]. And that [fruit] occurs only when the mind is constantly purified in this way, not spontaneously.

Alternatively, there is a reference to what was previously stated [in verse 79]: "He remains established in Brahman alone" (MDh 6.81). Abiding in Brahman is achieved through meditation (*dhyānika*), and not merely by the performance of ritual acts. To the question "What is that which is to be meditated upon?", he says: "For one who does not know the *adhyātma*. That which pertains to the Self (*ātman*)—such as the Vedānta and other texts—is *adhyātma*; he does not know this. Alternatively, that which is directed toward the Self is *adhyātma*, such as: "This Self is distinct from the body, senses, mind, intellect, vital breaths, and so forth; it does not perish when these perish; it is the agent of actions and the enjoyer of their fruits. All of this occurs for one who is drawn away by the perception of duality. But when this [Self] is free from evil (*apahatapāpman*), it is untouched by defects or effects; because of its oneness, this entire world is this very [Self], and there is nothing else distinct from it. Distinctness is a mere appearance. He who does not know the Upaniṣads—which describe [the Self] as having the color of the sun, being of the same essence as water, and so forth—and who does not produce firmness through meditation with one-pointed and continuous intelligence, does not obtain the fruit of action as described above. Therefore, the meaning of the verse is that the Self, whose nature is declared in the Vedānta, should be meditated upon constantly, except at the times of eating and recreation.

(3) Alternatively, even though the primary qualification belongs to the renunciant (*pravrajya*), there is nevertheless a mention of the householder as well, by way of his obtaining the fruit of ritual action, provided that action is predominant. Therefore, this is what is meant: although householders perform rituals such as the *agnihotra*, and are not knowers of the secret sciences (*rahasyavidyā*)—those sciences which are embedded within the rituals, such as the *udgītha* mentioned in the passage beginning with "Or, however many [sciences] follow the *udgītha*" (ChU 1.1.1)—even those who are experts in the *karmakāṇḍa* do not obtain from that a full fruit that persists for a long time. This point is demonstrated in two scriptural passages, one from the Vājasaneyaka and one from the Chāndogya: "O Gārgī, he who performs sacrifices, offers oblations, or practices austerities without knowing this Imperishable (*akṣara*), even if for many thousands of years, that [result] is indeed finite" (BĀU 3.8.10); and likewise, "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*), that alone becomes more powerful" (ChU 1.1.10). However, for one who performs [action] after having known the aforementioned science taught regarding the self (*adhyātma*), there is indeed an excellence of fruit. And it is said: "Now, those who know thus, and those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity... (ChU 5.10.1). Regarding those performers of action who possess such knowledge, the Scripture declares their attainment of the world of Brahman via the path of light (*arcirādi-mārga*) in the passage beginning with "He reaches" (ChU 5.10.1). 6.82.

Thus, since meditation on the object of contemplation has been prescribed for the sake of self-knowledge, the recitation of the Vedas was not previously established as a means to that end; therefore, he now prescribes it:

"One should constantly recite the Brahman pertaining to the sacrifice (adhiyajña), that which pertains to the deities (ādhidaivika), that which pertains to the self (ādhyātmika), and that which is declared in the Vedānta. (6.83)

For him, only the recitation (*japa*) is permitted, and not the study for the sake of practice as is the case for householders and others. Regarding sacrifices (*yajña*), there is the *adhvaryu* [portion], which is the prescriptive *brāhmaṇa*. Regarding the divine (*adhidaiva*), there are the mantras that reveal the deities. Their specific variety is the *ādhyātmika*, such as: "I became Manu... I [became] with the Rudras" (Ṛgveda 4.26.1), and so forth. That which is called *vedānta* also demonstrates the combination of ritual action and knowledge for the sake of attaining Brahmanhood. (6.83)
This is the refuge for the ignorant; this very thing is for those who understand.
This is for those seeking heaven; this is for those seeking the infinite.
He designates by "this" that which is called the Veda; that too is indeed Brahman. And thus it has been said:
"Two Brahmans are to be known: the Śabdabrahman and that which is the Parabrahman.
One who is proficient in the Śabdabrahman attains the Parabrahman. (MaitU 6.22)

"Study" means understanding; it is proficiency gained through the performance of its prescribed meaning. This is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the preceding injunction. It refers to those who are ignorant—that is, those who do not know the meaning of the Veda—since they are entitled to perform recitations (*japa*) and the like. Accordingly, the venerable Vyāsa has demonstrated that success (*siddhi*) is attained by those who recite. Alternatively, "the ignorant" are those who lack self-knowledge (*anātmajña*), who have not understood the reality of the Self through the scriptures, yet are devoted to its meditation; though they have not yet attained stability of mind, for them the Veda is a refuge. Through recitation, the performance of rituals, and such knowledge, they avoid rebirth in hells or among insects, moths, and other such lower forms of existence.

This indeed is for those who understand. But how is it a refuge for the wise? To this he says: "for those seeking heaven. Those experts in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) whose minds have not yet found firm rest in the Self obtain results such as heaven through the performance of rituals. Others, however, having abandoned attachment and whose defects such as passion have been destroyed, are devoted to the meditation on the reality of the Self through knowledge; for them there is infinity, meaning non-return [to saṃsāra]. The meaning is that for all, the Veda alone is the refuge; there is no other path. (6.84)
The twice-born man who wanders forth as a mendicant according to this sequential method,
having shaken off all evil in this world, attains the supreme Brahman.

"Gradually" refers to the practice of yoga. The meaning is that one should discharge one's debts by following the sequence previously stated for the combination of self-knowledge and ritual action (*karma*). Having shaken off evil, like a horse shakes off the dust from its hair, so too does one shake it off through the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*), as it is said: "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, so evil action does not cling to one who knows this" (ChU 4.14.3). One attains the Supreme Brahman; becoming of that very nature, with the perception of duality ceased—this is the injunction regarding the fruit of knowledge and the stages of life (*āśrama*). 6.85.
This is the dharma taught to you for those ascetics of restrained self who have renounced the Vedas; now learn the yoga of action.

The renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) of the Veda means its abandonment; those who possess this are the "Veda-renouncers" (*vedasaṃnyāsikāḥ*). By the word "Veda," the abandonment of ritual acts such as sacrifices and oblations is intended, but not the abandonment of silent recitation (*japa*). However, reflection on the Self (*ātmacintana*) is indeed enjoined. Only those rites achievable through wealth or bodily hardship—such as pilgrimages and fasting—are prohibited. As for those rites that can be accomplished solely by means of the Self, such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) and silent recitation, there is no prohibition of them. We shall demonstrate this in its proper place. With the first half-verse, the stage of wandering mendicancy (*pravrajyāśrama*) is concluded; with the latter, there is the promise to teach the duties of the Veda-renouncer. (6.86)
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—these four distinct stages of life originate from the householder. (6.87)
When all these are practiced in succession according to the scriptures, they lead the brahmin who acts as prescribed to the supreme goal. (6.88)

But surely, given the promise "I shall describe the duties of the renunciant (saṃnyāsika)," the enumeration of the stages of life (āśrama) is irrelevant to the context. Some say: no, it is not so; rather, this is intended to show that renunciation is not a separate stage of life, but is included within this very one. And in which [stage] is it included? It is included within the householder's stage, for his dwelling is indeed in the home.

Others, however, [place it] among the stages of renunciation (*pravrajyā*), because of the commonality of abandoning attachments. Therefore, there is no need for its inclusion [among the other stages]. It will not be qualified for sacrifices and the like by the duties of a man (*puruṣadharma*) or the duties of an ascetic (*yatidharma*), because these are prescribed by their own specific terms. If it is argued that, since he is not in a stage of life (*anāśramitvāt*), the contingency of penance would arise according to the rule, "One who remains without a stage of life for a year [must perform penance]," we reply: since this very regulation is known through scripture itself, how can there be any occasion for penance?

Therefore, the mention of the other stages of life (*āśrama*) is for the purpose of praising the renunciant by way of his equality with the householder and others; and that is intended to confirm their combination. The meaning is that these [other stages] have their existence in the householders. The analysis of the compound is: "the householder is the source (*prabhava*), the cause of their subsistence. (6.87–88)
And among all these [stages of life], according to the injunctions of Vedic revelation,
the householder is said to be the best, for he indeed supports these other three.

This is improper. By the Vedic revelation (*veda-śruti*), the injunction for the householder’s stage (*gārhasthya*) is established, as is the obligation to support the others. The very existence of the other stages of life (*āśrama*) is due precisely to the injunction of the householder’s stage found in direct revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*). Revelation is more powerful than the Smṛtis concerning austerity (*tapas*) which are proximate [in authority]. Now, if it be argued: "This connection—that [the others] are not enjoined by Vedic revelation—is not being made," this is the connection: even if this injunction for the householder exists, his preeminence (*śraiṣṭhya*) is established by the phrase "he supports these three" (*sa trīn etān*) on account of his supporting them; in that case, it must be asked: how so, since the other stages are also revealed? And if they are revealed, this Smṛti is clearly contradicted by such statements as: "Because of the direct injunction of the householder’s stage" (GDh 3.36). Nor is another possible connection feasible. If it be argued: "Having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller; having been a forest-dweller, one should renounce"—relying on this Jābāla Śruti, all [stages] are indeed revealed—then the contradiction with Smṛti remains entirely unrefuted. Furthermore, this Śruti is not injunctive. For it is not heard there: "In this way one should roam in the forest," or "These specific duties are to be performed by the forest-dweller, and these by the renunciant," in the manner that every duty of the householder—from the giving of gifts up to the final sacrifice (*antyeṣṭi*)—is directly stated. It is not so for the other stages; only their mere names are heard, such as "having been a householder," and so forth. Therefore, it is taught as if the stages have the householder’s stage as their root, though this is contradictory from beginning to end.

To this it is replied: It is true that, from the time of the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) onwards, household duties are directly enjoined by scripture for one who has taken a wife. In that regard, since the motive (*prayukti*) must be determined for marriage, by what is the action enjoined by the scriptures? Is it by the scriptural injunction regarding the qualification for the *agnihotra* and other rites, or by the injunction for the procreation of offspring, or else by a visible human purpose?

But surely, passion impels one toward a woman in general, not toward marriage; for there is the principle that "that without which something cannot be accomplished is the motivator of that thing. And since those possessed by passion can accomplish the domestic rites (*gṛhyakarman*) by means of a woman in general, why would they require marriage?

True; if going to any woman whatsoever were forbidden by another statement [of scripture]. Even though the acquisition of the Veda is common to all, the distinction between those who may be approached and those who may not is established by the treatises (*śāstra*). Therefore, since for those of a resolute nature there is no fulfillment of their own purpose without marriage, the suspicion that the Veda is the motivating factor is indeed appropriate.

If this is so, then there are no instigating factors for everyone; since the purpose is accomplished for all when that [marriage] exists, what is the point of defining it? Let that which is the instigator of marriage be so. But as for the inquiry into the instigation of marriage, how does it relate to the discussion of how the other stages of life (*āśrama*) are possible given the direct injunction for the householder stage?
It is said in reply: it relates to the point already stated—that the accomplishment of the purpose belongs to all.

True. When one [act] has been performed and the assistance for another is accomplished by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*), there is no assumption of a separate performance. For example, rice grains, already employed for the human purpose of subsistence, are subsequently applied to ritual acts; yet the acquisition of wealth is not separately enjoined for the sake of the ritual. Or again, even though the status of being a Vedic scholar (*vaidya*) exists, the learning of the Vedas is not separately enjoined, because that is already accomplished by the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*). Likewise, since activity here is established through desire, the scriptural injunctions regarding ritual acts need not be separately enjoined. Therefore, the injunctions for obligatory duties (*kṛtyakarman*) will apply even to one who has not yet married.

And therefore, one who has somehow become matured in his impurities (*kaṣāya*) while still in the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*) does not desire [to marry]. Consequently, due to the absence of a second [partner], he will not be eligible [for ritual action]. And thus, because of the lack of eligibility for the Vedic rites, such a person would fall into another stage of life (*āśrama*).

Others think: "This marriage is not comparable to wealth. Just as life is impossible without wealth—since one indeed lives by means of wealth—even so there is no absence of life without a woman; therefore, no visible purpose for the self-restrained person is possible. Thus, marriage is undertaken even for the sake of eligibility for religious duty (*dharma*). And this must necessarily be understood in this way: that an effort must be made for the sake of producing eligibility. For otherwise, if eligibility were lost due to impurity following an emission (*utsarga*), then for one who performs the purification rites at the proper time after birth and so forth, there would be no transgression of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*). Consequently, for what purpose would he undergo the hardship of purification after death and the like? If it is argued that even that [purification] is prescribed, [we reply: in that case, there would be a transgression of only that much, and not of a thousand other injunctions.

Now, it might be argued: "Of which injunction (*vidhi*) is this the operation, such that it teaches that a person must exert effort so as to think, 'I shall become qualified' for the sake of accomplishing qualification? [The answer is: The injunctions regarding the *agnihotra* and other rites merely convey that those for whom the Vedic tradition has been handed down possess a duty (*kartavyatā*) with respect to those subjects; they do not, however, enjoin the production of the fires (*agni*). Even the fires are studied by one who proceeds toward optional rites (*kāmya*) out of desire, for the sake of establishing his qualification for them. For when those fires have been produced, there are scriptural texts concerning lifelong performance based on the state of being one who has established the fires (*āhitāgni*). Furthermore, one is qualified for the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) only if he possesses a wife. Just as he establishes the fires to make himself a qualified agent, so too does he marry a wife. Therefore, no purpose of any injunction remains unfulfilled if the qualification for the *agnihotra* and other rites is not to be generated. Nor does the injunction regarding marriage itself convey that its own purpose is a duty to be performed, because it is a sacramental act (*saṃskārakarma*) and lacks any mention of a specific qualification (*adhikāra*), unlike the scriptural texts for the obligatory *agnihotra* and other rites.

On this point, the ancients say: There is a scriptural text regarding the discharge of the three debts, beginning with, “A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is indeed born with three debts” (TS 6.3.10.5). This scriptural statement refers to the state of being born. Nor is the second birth here intended—the one called initiation (*upanayana*)—because prior to that, one possesses the same characteristics as animals. What is grasped by the scriptural mention of the debt is precisely that period of time following birth during which the understanding of one’s entitlement (*adhikāra*) arises. Consequently, for one who is learned and possesses such entitlement, if he should not obtain a girl when asking for her hand, his entitlement to the forest-dweller stage (*vānaprastha*) and so forth occurs only when he is completely grey-haired. For he determines this: “While still in youth, I asked for a girl in every way. Others say: “The laying of the fires (*ādhāna*) is heard [to be prescribed] only for one with black hair; except in the case of a wife’s death, one with completely grey hair must not lay the fires”—thus they explain the meaning of the scripture.

Because of his connection with ritual action (*karman*), the householder is superior; thus, the superiority of the stage of life itself has been stated. Regarding the phrase "these three": this is another reason for its superiority, namely that it supports the other stages of life. This has been stated [in verse 3.68]: "By means of knowledge and by means of food. (MDh 3.68) || 6.89 ||
This very point is confirmed by means of an illustration:
"Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean, even so do all those in the [other] stages of life find their resting place in the householder. (6.90)

The rivers are the Gaṅgā and others; the streams are the Bhidya and others. The distinction in the designation of "river" (nadī) and "stream" (nada) is due to a certain difference in the arrangement of their channels and a difference in their flow. Their designation as a single entity, however, is by way of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). The difference in gender is like that between the words *bhāryā* and *dāra*. "Abode" (*saṃsthiti*) means the support. Just as the ocean is the support for all waters, so the householder has authority over all dharmas. 6.90.
Moreover, by these four classes of twice-born men belonging to the various stages of life, the tenfold dharma must always be practiced with diligent effort. (6.91)

This verse is intended as an introduction to what is about to be said. "That which has ten characteristics" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) here means essential nature (*svarūpa*). It "should be practiced at all times," meaning it is to be performed continuously. These [virtues] are mentioned again despite having been previously stated in order to emphasize their preeminence. Furthermore, by this repetition, the position that there is a synthesis of knowledge and action (*jñāna-karma-samuccaya*) is reinforced. (6.91)
Fortitude, forgiveness, self-restraint, non-stealing, purity, control of the senses, wisdom, learning, truthfulness, and freedom from anger—this is the tenfold characteristic of dharma. 6.92

Fortitude (*dhṛti*) and the others are qualities of the self (*ātman*). Among them, fortitude is the reliance upon one's own being (*sattva*) when wealth and such are depleted; it is the thought: "If it is exhausted, what of it? It can be acquired again. Likewise, it is the stabilization of the mind—which would otherwise waver due to separation from the beloved and so forth—by reflecting that "this is the nature of the course of saṃsāra. Patience (*kṣamā*) is the endurance of offenses; it is the absence of agitation or retaliation toward someone who has committed a wrong. Self-restraint (*dama*) is the absence of arrogance and the renunciation of pride in learning and the like. Non-stealing (*asteya*) is well known. Purity (*śauca*) is the purification of food and other such things. Control of the senses (*indriyasaṃyama*) is non-attachment even to objects that are not forbidden. Wisdom (*dhī*) is right knowledge, which dispels opposing views, doubt, and so forth. Knowledge (*vidyā*) is the knowledge of the self (*ātman*). The distinction between wisdom and knowledge is based on the division between knowledge of ritual action (*karman*) and knowledge of the inner self (*adhyātma*). Some read "wisdom and knowledge" (*dhīvidyā*) as a single term to avoid redundancy; however, that is not correct, because the distinction has already been shown. The rest is well known. Absence of anger (*akrodha*) is the non-arising of anger that is about to arise. Patience (*kṣamā*) is the non-commencement of harm even when harm has been done [to oneself]. (6.92)
Those brahmins who thoroughly study the ten characteristics of dharma, and having studied them, live in accordance with them, attain the supreme goal. (6.93)
This is the statement of the fruit for the preceding injunction: the mention of the fruit resulting from study is intended to signify the necessity of performing the rite. 6.93.
Practicing the Dharma characterized by the ten marks with a concentrated mind,
and having heard the Vedānta according to the injunctions, the twice-born man, free from debts, should renounce.

"One should renounce when free from debt. This means that renunciation occurs only when the three debts have been discharged; one is not entitled to the life of a wandering mendicant (*pravrajyā*) at any other time, and the same applies to renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). "The Vedāntas according to rule": for one who has not understood the meaning of the Vedāntas, there is no renunciation. Although knowledge of the Vedāntas is—like ritual action—implied by the performance of the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), since both are equally denoted by the term *svādhyāya*, the Vedāntas are mentioned again for a specific purpose. One must be devoted to them.
Now, what is the meaning of the scriptural injunction "one should renounce" (*saṃnyaset*)? What indeed is this so-called renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*)?
It is the abandonment of the sense of possession, such as "this is mine.

But is it not said, "those who have renounced the Vedas" (*vedasaṃnyāsikāḥ*) [Manu Dharmaśāstra 6.86]? In that context, it would appear to mean the renunciation of the Veda or the meaning of the Veda; it does not mean the renunciation of those acts such as receiving gifts which are for the sake of accomplishing Vedic rites.

Because [the rule] "this is for those who desire infinity" (MDh 6.84) prescribes study even when knowledge is the primary goal, whereas the Agnihotra and other such rites are accomplished through material substances (*dravya*), their renunciation occurs only in the absence of the sense of ownership (*mamakāra*). Furthermore, this renunciation—which brings about *dharma*—applies to one whose wife has died, to one who has attained the highest state, or to one who has made the necessary arrangements. For it is recited in the Vājasaneyaka: "When he thinks he is about to depart, then he says to his son," and so forth. And the consigning of the sacred fires (*agnisamāropaṇa*) is prescribed at that time for one who is not yet infirm; for they declare: "One is indeed released from this by old age. As for those rites that do not require material substances, such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsanā*) and the obligatory Agnihotra, there is no prohibition against them; therefore, one remains qualified in those until the very last breath. (6.94)
Having renounced all actions and cast off the defects of action, let him, self-restrained, study the Veda and dwell happily under the sovereignty of his sons. (6.95)

"Let him study the Veda"—by this he states that one must not abandon the Veda; this has already been demonstrated. Alternatively, there is a reading ending in the present participle suffix *śatṛ*: "while studying. "He may live happily under the authority of his son": the mention of the "son" refers to a son who has been born. Others say that even for another person who occupies that position, such as a city-dweller (*paura*) or similar, the relinquishing of the house is likewise appropriate. (6.95)
Having thus renounced all actions, intent upon his own duty and free from longing, he destroys sin through such renunciation and attains the supreme goal. (6.96)
"Devoted to his own duty" means one for whom the supreme primary task is the worship of the Self. "Free from longing" means that no desire whatsoever should be entertained even by the mind. (6.96)
This fourfold dharma of the Brāhmaṇa has been declared to you;
it is meritorious and yields imperishable fruit after death. Now learn the dharma of kings.
The Dharma is fourfold, consisting of the four stages of life; all of this is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa.

But surely, the term "twice-born" (*dvija*) is heard at the beginning [of the section]: "Thus, having remained in the householder stage, a twice-born man who has performed the ritual bath according to rule... (MDh 6.1). Since no contradiction has yet arisen, it is certain that this refers to members of all three *varṇas*. Therefore, it is appropriate that this mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is intended merely to illustrate the three *varṇas*. This would not be the case if there were not a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*) between the opening and the conclusion; but since there is such unity, the meaning of the opening, being more powerful, is what must be understood.

The meaning is determined by a comprehensive consideration of the entire statement. Therefore, the mention of the *dvija* (twice-born) must be restricted to the *brāhmaṇa*. While a *brāhmaṇa* possesses the status of being twice-born, not all twice-born persons possess *brāhmaṇya* (the state of being a Brahmin). Furthermore, when the primary meaning of the word *dvija* is possible, it is not proper to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for something that lacks connection [to the context]. Moreover, in the *Mahābhārata*, the three stages of life (*āśrama*) are heard of even for the *śūdra*: beginning with "for one who has fulfilled his duty through service," it says, "all stages of life are prescribed, excluding the meatless [stage]" (MBh 12.63.12–13). This refers to the stage of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*). It does not mean that all stages of life are not to be undertaken; rather, through service and the procreation of offspring, he obtains the fruit of all stages of life. By serving the twice-born while remaining in the householder stage, he obtains the fruit of all stages of life, excluding the liberation that is the fruit of the wandering mendicant.
Therefore, it is established that the four stages of life (cāturāśramya) constitute the very dharma of the Brahmin. 6.97.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Thus ends the sixth chapter of the Commentary on Manu, composed by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi, son of Bhaṭṭa Vīrasvāmin.
